What it shows — Coaches by type; the total was 91,948 in 2023-24 including rail cars.

How to read it — Other coaching vehicles grew fastest, by 14%; passenger carriages grew 0.5%.

Why it matters — Coach numbers limit how many passengers can be carried.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Other Important Statistics, number of coaches (2022-23 revised); Year Book 2023-24, pp. 4-6.

indicators.title: Wagon Fleet
indicators.subtitle: Freight wagons owned by Indian Railways
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total wagons owned by Indian Railways.

How to read it — The fleet grew by 12,888 wagons (4.1%) to 327,991.

Why it matters — Wagon availability caps freight loading.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Other Important Statistics, number of wagons (2022-23 revised); Year Book 2023-24, pp. 4-6.

indicators.title: Wagon Turn-Round Time
indicators.subtitle: Days for a wagon to complete a loading cycle
indicators.details:
What it shows — Average days for a broad-gauge wagon to complete one loading cycle.

How to read it — Turn-round lengthened from 4.70 to 5.11 days.

Why it matters — A shorter turn-round lets the same fleet carry more freight.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Other Important Statistics, Wagon Utilisation (broad gauge); Year Book 2023-24, pp. 4-6.

indicators.title: Average Goods Train Load
indicators.subtitle: Net and gross load per goods train
indicators.details:
What it shows — Average net and gross load of a broad-gauge goods train.

How to read it — Net load per train rose 9.3% to 1,899 tonnes, while average goods-train speed fell to 25.0 km/h.

Why it matters — Heavier trains move more per path, but slower speeds lengthen transit times.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Other Important Statistics, goods train utilisation (broad gauge, all traction). Average goods-train speed fell from 30.8 to 25.0 km/h over the same year; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 4-6.

indicators.title: Locomotive Fleet by Traction Share
indicators.subtitle: Electric, diesel and steam shares
indicators.details:
What it shows — Locomotive counts by traction as a share of all reported electric, diesel and steam locomotives.

How to read it — Electric locomotives were 70.65% of the listed fleet in 2023-24.

Why it matters — Shares make the traction transition comparable despite fleet growth.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Other Important Statistics, locomotive counts by traction on 31 March 2023 and 31 March 2024; shares calculated from category totals; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 4-6.

indicators.title: Share of Listed Coach Categories
indicators.subtitle: Composition of the three reported coach groups
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of passenger carriages, other coaching vehicles and EMU/MEMU coaches among those listed categories.

How to read it — Passenger carriages were 72.53% of the listed 2023-24 categories.

Why it matters — Category shares show how the reported coaching fleet is composed.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Other Important Statistics, number of coaches by category, 2022-23 revised and 2023-24; shares calculated over the three listed categories; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 4-6.

indicators.title: Goods Trains as Share of Daily Trains
indicators.subtitle: Goods trains among reported passenger and goods trains
indicators.details:
What it shows — Goods trains run daily divided by the combined daily passenger and goods train counts.

How to read it — Goods trains made up 47.04% of the two reported train groups in 2023-24.

Why it matters — The mix compares passenger and freight operating intensity.

datasets.label: Goods Trains as Share of Daily Trains

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Other Important Statistics, daily passenger and goods trains run; goods share calculated from the two reported totals; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 4-6.

indicators.title: Average Net Load as Share of Gross Load
indicators.subtitle: Net tonnes per goods train relative to gross tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Average net goods-train load divided by average gross load.

How to read it — The net-to-gross ratio was 61.56% in 2023-24.

Why it matters — The ratio shows the share of average gross train weight represented by payload.

datasets.label: Average Net Load as Share of Gross Load

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Other Important Statistics, average net and gross goods-train loads; net-to-gross ratios calculated from the reported values; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 4-6.

indicators.title: Consequential Train Accidents by Type
indicators.subtitle: Accidents per year, 2019-20 to 2023-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — Consequential train accidents split into derailments, collisions, fires, level-crossing and other accidents.

How to read it — Derailments are the largest category (25 of 40 in 2023-24); fire accidents rose to 9.

Why it matters — Type-wise counts show where safety work matters most.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Safety, consequential train accidents by type, including Konkan Railway; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 52-59.

indicators.title: Total Consequential Train Accidents
indicators.subtitle: Accidents per year
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total consequential train accidents.

How to read it — 40 in 2023-24, against 55 in 2019-20 and 48 in 2022-23.

Why it matters — Raw counts show how many serious incidents occurred.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Safety, total consequential train accidents including Konkan Railway; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 52-59.

indicators.title: Accidents per Million Train-Km
indicators.subtitle: Accident rate normalised for traffic
indicators.details:
What it shows — Consequential accidents divided by million train-kilometres run.

How to read it — The rate has held at 0.03 since 2020-21, against 0.05 in 2019-20.

Why it matters — A rate shows safety per unit of traffic, unlike a raw count.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Safety, accidents per million train kilometres, the Year Book's principal safety index; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 52-59.

indicators.title: Accident Types (2023-24)
indicators.subtitle: Composition of 40 consequential accidents
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of each accident type among the 40 consequential accidents in 2023-24.

How to read it — Derailments are 62.5%, fires 22.5% and collisions 15%.

Why it matters — Shows which accident types dominate.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Safety, 2023-24: 40 consequential accidents; none at level crossings or miscellaneous; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 52-59.

indicators.title: Derailments and Collisions
indicators.subtitle: Combined derailment and collision counts
indicators.details:
What it shows — Yearly derailment and collision counts added together from the consequential-accident table.

How to read it — There were 31 derailments and collisions in 2023-24.

Why it matters — These two accident types together account for a large share of consequential incidents.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Safety, consequential train accidents table; derailments plus collisions calculated from the listed types; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 52-59.

indicators.title: Derailments as Share of Consequential Accidents
indicators.subtitle: Derailments divided by all listed consequential accidents
indicators.details:
What it shows — Derailments as a percentage of all consequential train accidents listed for each year.

How to read it — Derailments accounted for 62.50% of consequential accidents in 2023-24.

Why it matters — The share distinguishes the leading accident type from the overall count.

datasets.label: Derailments as Share of Consequential Accidents

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Safety, consequential train accidents table; derailments divided by each year's total; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 52-59.

indicators.title: Year-on-Year Accident Count Change
indicators.subtitle: Percent change in consequential accident totals
indicators.details:
What it shows — Year-on-year percentage change in the sum of the five reported accident categories.

How to read it — The total changed by -16.67% between 2022-23 and 2023-24.

Why it matters — Year-on-year change shows direction as well as scale.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Safety, consequential train accidents table; year-on-year changes calculated from the sum of listed accident types; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 52-59.

indicators.title: Railway Revenue and Expenses
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, 2022-23 and 2023-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total revenue, expenses and net revenue of Indian Railways.

How to read it — Revenue rose 6.4% to Rs 2.55 lakh crore; expenses rose 6.5%, leaving Rs 3,260 crore of net revenue.

Why it matters — Net revenue is small relative to turnover.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Key Statistics, financial results; Year Book 2023-24, p. 3.

indicators.title: Passenger vs Freight Earnings
indicators.subtitle: Earnings by business, Rs crore
indicators.details:
What it shows — Earnings from passenger and freight services.

How to read it — Passenger earnings grew 11.5% and freight 3.6%; freight is 70% of the two combined.

Why it matters — Freight is the larger earner.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Passenger Business and Freight Operation, earnings (freight excludes demurrage and wharfage); Year Book 2023-24, pp. 22-45.

indicators.title: Operating and Working Ratios
indicators.subtitle: Expenses as a percentage of earnings
indicators.details:
What it shows — Operating ratio is expenditure as a share of earnings; lower is better.

How to read it — The overall ratio was 98.43%. Goods runs at 67.55% while coaching is 177.69%, meaning Rs 1.78 is spent for every Re 1 earned from passengers.

Why it matters — The ratio shows how much of each rupee earned is left for investment.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Some Selected Financial Ratio; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 7-8.

indicators.title: Passenger and Freight Yield
indicators.subtitle: Average revenue per unit of traffic
indicators.details:
What it shows — Average revenue per passenger-km and per net tonne-km.

How to read it — Passenger yield was 66.40 paise per passenger-km and freight 170.31 paise per net tonne-km.

Why it matters — Yield compares what the railway earns on each unit of traffic.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Some Selected Financial Ratio, earning/yield ratios based on apportioned earning; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 7-8.

indicators.title: Passenger and Freight Earnings Shares
indicators.subtitle: Share of combined passenger and freight earnings
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passenger and freight earnings as percentages of the two categories' combined earnings.

How to read it — Freight represented 70.12% of combined passenger and freight earnings in 2023-24.

Why it matters — The shares show the relative contribution of the two main traffic earnings streams.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Passenger Business and Freight Operation earnings table; shares calculated over those two earning streams; Year Book 2023-24, pp. 22-45.

indicators.title: Net Revenue Margin
indicators.subtitle: Net revenue as a share of total revenue
indicators.details:
What it shows — Reported net revenue divided by total railway revenue for each year.

How to read it — Net revenue was 1.28% of total revenue in 2023-24.

Why it matters — The margin shows the net result relative to the scale of railway earnings.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Key Statistics, financial results; net revenue divided by total revenue; Year Book 2023-24, p. 3.

indicators.title: Revenue and Expense Growth
indicators.subtitle: Year-on-year change in railway revenue and expenses
indicators.details:
What it shows — Percentage change in reported total revenue and total expenses from 2022-23 to 2023-24.

How to read it — Revenue increased 6.37%; expenses increased 6.47%.

Why it matters — Comparing the two growth rates shows whether expenses grew faster than revenue.

series.note: Ministry of Railways, Indian Railways Year Book 2023-24 (Directorate of Statistics & Economics, Railway Board): Key Statistics, financial results; growth rates calculated from reported total revenue and expenses; Year Book 2023-24, p. 3.

indicators.title: Passengers Handled: Domestic vs International
indicators.subtitle: All Indian airports, 2022-23 and 2023-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passenger traffic handled at all Indian airports, split between domestic and international.

How to read it — Total traffic grew 15.0% to 376.43 million; international grew 22.3% against 13.5% for domestic.

Why it matters — International traffic was still catching up after COVID-19, so it grew faster.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Board's Report, traffic handled at all Indian airports. Passengers are counted as movements, arrivals plus departures.

indicators.title: Aircraft Movements: Domestic vs International
indicators.subtitle: Takeoffs and landings, thousands
indicators.details:
What it shows — Aircraft movements (takeoffs and landings) at all Indian airports.

How to read it — Movements grew 6.7% to 2,677.59 thousand, slower than passengers: international movements rose 16.5%, domestic 5.1%.

Why it matters — Passengers growing faster than movements means aircraft are flying fuller or larger.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Board's Report, aircraft movements at all Indian airports.

indicators.title: Domestic vs International Passengers (2023-24)
indicators.subtitle: Share of 376.43 million passengers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Domestic and international share of 2023-24 airport passenger traffic.

How to read it — Domestic is 81.5% and international 18.5%.

Why it matters — India's air market is predominantly domestic.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Board's Report, 2023-24 passengers at all Indian airports.

indicators.title: Domestic vs International Movements (2023-24)
indicators.subtitle: Share of 2,677.59 thousand movements
indicators.details:
What it shows — Domestic and international share of 2023-24 aircraft movements.

How to read it — Domestic is 84.1% and international 15.9%.

Why it matters — International flights carry more passengers per movement than domestic ones.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Board's Report, 2023-24 aircraft movements at all Indian airports.

indicators.title: Scheduled Passengers Carried to 2024-25
indicators.subtitle: Passengers on scheduled airlines, Ministry of Civil Aviation
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passengers carried on scheduled domestic and international flights.

How to read it — Scheduled domestic passengers grew 7.7% to 165.5 million in 2024-25; international rose to 74.14 million.

Why it matters — Brings the passenger series up to 2024-25, past the AAI report's year.

series.note: Ministry of Civil Aviation performance summary (https://www.civilaviation.gov.in/our-performance) and Lok Sabha reply of 4 December 2025 (https://www.sansad.in/getFile/loksabhaquestions/annex/186/AU861_6WIzEa.pdf?source=pqals): 165.5 million domestic and 74.14 million international passengers on scheduled flights in 2024-25, against 153.7 and 66.8 million in 2023-24. These count passengers carried by scheduled airlines, so they are lower than AAI's movement-based totals.

indicators.title: Domestic vs International Passengers, 2018-19 to 2025-26
indicators.subtitle: Million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Domestic and international passengers at all Indian airports, financial years.

How to read it — International fell to 10.1 million in 2020-21 (from 69.5) and reached 80.6 million in 2025-26; domestic reached 339.4 million.

Why it matters — Shows how differently the two segments fell and recovered.

series.note: AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2023-24 (Board's Report traffic tables) and AAI Traffic News March 2026 (2024-25 and 2025-26).

indicators.title: Domestic vs International Aircraft Movements
indicators.subtitle: Thousand, 2018-19 to 2025-26
indicators.details:
What it shows — Domestic and international takeoffs and landings by financial year.

How to read it — International movements are 481 thousand in 2025-26, +6.3% against 2018-19; domestic +12.6%.

Why it matters — Movement counts show real flight activity regardless of seat size.

series.note: AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2023-24 and AAI Traffic News March 2026, aircraft movements at all Indian airports.

indicators.title: International Share of Passengers
indicators.subtitle: % of all airport passengers
indicators.details:
What it shows — International passengers as a share of all passengers.

How to read it — 20.2% in 2018-19, 8.8% in 2020-21 and 19.2% in 2025-26.

Why it matters — Tracks how quickly international travel regains its pre-pandemic weight.

series.note: Computed from international and total passengers in AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2023-24 and AAI Traffic News March 2026.

indicators.title: Busiest International Airports (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: International passengers, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — International passengers at the ten busiest international gateways.

How to read it — Delhi leads at 21.55 million (29.9% of the 10 shown); Kolkata is lowest at 2.30 million.

Why it matters — International traffic is concentrated at metro and Kerala airports.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise international passengers.

indicators.title: Busiest Domestic Airports (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Domestic passengers, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Domestic passengers at the ten busiest airports.

How to read it — Delhi leads at 57.15 million (25.0% of the 10 shown); Kochi is lowest at 5.97 million.

Why it matters — Domestic traffic is dominated by the metros plus Pune and Guwahati.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise domestic passengers.

indicators.title: International Passengers by State (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Top ten states, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — International passengers by the state in which the airport is located.

How to read it — Delhi leads at 21.55 million (27.4% of the 10 shown); Punjab is lowest at 1.00 million.

Why it matters — Shows which states are India's international gateways.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure VI: state-wise traffic (international passengers).

indicators.title: Domestic vs International Passengers by Region
indicators.subtitle: AAI regions, 2025-26, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passengers in each AAI region split into domestic and international.

How to read it — Southern region has 41.4% of international passengers; North East is almost entirely domestic.

Why it matters — Shows the regional balance between domestic and overseas travel.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure V: region-wise traffic.

indicators.title: Monthly Domestic and International Passengers
indicators.subtitle: 2025 vs 2026, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Monthly domestic and international passengers, this year and last.

How to read it — September 2026: domestic 24.00 million (-6.3%), international 6.10 million (-4.2%).

Why it matters — Shows which segment drives the monthly changes.

series.note: AAI monthly Traffic News reports, January to September 2026 against the same months of 2025.

indicators.title: Domestic Passengers by Airline (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Calendar year 2024, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Domestic passengers carried by each Indian scheduled airline in 2024.

How to read it — IndiGo carried 99.9 million, 61.9% of the 161.3 million total.

Why it matters — Airline concentration shapes fares and capacity.

series.note: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 4389 (27 March 2025), Ministry of Civil Aviation: domestic passengers carried by each scheduled airline, 2023 and 2024.

indicators.title: Domestic Airline Market Share (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Share of 161.3 million domestic passengers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Each airline's share of domestic passengers in 2024.

How to read it — IndiGo holds 61.9% and Air India 12.1%.

Why it matters — Market share shows how competitive the domestic market is.

series.note: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 4389 (27 March 2025): airline-wise domestic passengers; shown are the six largest airlines and all others combined (grand total from the annexure).

indicators.title: Airline Domestic Passenger Growth (2024 vs 2023)
indicators.subtitle: Airlines with over 1 million passengers in 2023
indicators.details:
What it shows — Year-on-year change in each large airline's domestic passengers.

How to read it — Air India grew +36.2%, IndiGo +8.7% and SpiceJet -28.4%.

Why it matters — Shows which airlines gained and lost domestic traffic.

series.note: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 4389: percentage change computed from each airline's 2023 and 2024 domestic passengers (airlines under 1 million in 2023 or absent in 2024 are left out).

indicators.title: Domestic Passengers by Quarter
indicators.subtitle: 2023 vs 2024, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Domestic passengers in each calendar quarter.

How to read it — 2024 total 161.3 million, +6.1% on 2023; the October-December quarter was highest at 42.8 million.

Why it matters — Shows the winter peak in October-December.

series.note: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 4389: quarterly domestic passengers, grand totals for 2023 and 2024.

indicators.title: International Passengers by Airline (2024-25)
indicators.subtitle: Provisional, up to October 2024, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — International passengers carried by Indian airlines in 2024-25.

How to read it — IndiGo carried 7.8 million of 19.0 million; Air India group airlines carried 8.6 million.

Why it matters — Shows how concentrated overseas flying is among a few carriers.

series.note: Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question 2260 (16 December 2024), Ministry of Civil Aviation: operator-wise domestic and international passengers for 2024-25 (provisional).

indicators.title: On-Time Performance by Airline (2024)
indicators.subtitle: % of flights on time
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of flights that left on schedule, by airline.

How to read it — Akasa Air leads at 73.3%; SpiceJet is lowest at 52.3%.

Why it matters — Punctuality is a core passenger-experience measure.

series.note: Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question 2419 (11 August 2025), Ministry of Civil Aviation: on-time performance of scheduled airlines, calendar 2024.

indicators.title: On-Time Performance by Airline (2025 to 30 June)
indicators.subtitle: % of flights on time
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of flights that left on schedule in the first half of 2025.

How to read it — IndiGo leads at 82.4%; Alliance Air is lowest at 58.1%.

Why it matters — Shows whether punctuality has improved since 2024.

datasets.label: On-Time Performance by Airline (2025 to 30 June)

series.note: Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question 2419: on-time performance, January to 30 June 2025; Air India Group includes Air India Express.

indicators.title: Flight Cancellation Rate by Airline (2024)
indicators.subtitle: % of scheduled flights cancelled
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of scheduled flights cancelled.

How to read it — Alliance Air leads at 4.2%; Akasa Air is lowest at 0.4%.

Why it matters — High cancellation rates mark weaker regional operators.

series.note: Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question 2419: cancellation rates of scheduled airlines, calendar 2024.

indicators.title: Flight Cancellation Rate by Airline (2025 to 30 June)
indicators.subtitle: % of scheduled flights cancelled
indicators.details:
What it shows — Share of scheduled flights cancelled in the first half of 2025.

How to read it — Alliance Air leads at 4.9%; Akasa Air is lowest at 0.3%.

Why it matters — Compares reliability across airlines.

datasets.label: Flight Cancellation Rate by Airline (2025 to 30 June)

series.note: Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question 2419: cancellation rates, January to 30 June 2025; Air India Group includes Air India Express.

indicators.title: Aircraft Movements Since 2018-19
indicators.subtitle: Aircraft movements, thousands
indicators.details:
What it shows — Aircraft movements reported by AAI each year.

How to read it — Movements fell to 1,196.74 thousand in 2020-21 and reached 2,677.59 thousand in 2023-24, above the 2018-19 level of 2,605.96 thousand.

Why it matters — Shows the COVID-19 collapse and the full recovery of flying.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Performance at a Glance, aircraft movements at AAI-reporting airports, six years.

indicators.title: Busiest Airports by Passengers (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Top ten airports, million passengers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total passengers (arrivals plus departures) at the ten busiest Indian airports in April-March 2025-26.

How to read it — Delhi leads with 78.7 million; the ten airports together handle 70.4% of all 420.1 million passengers.

Why it matters — Passenger traffic is concentrated at a few hub airports, which sets where capacity is needed.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise passenger traffic (domestic plus international). Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad are the JV airports MIAL, BIAL and GHIAL.

indicators.title: Busiest Airports: 2024-25 vs 2025-26
indicators.subtitle: Million passengers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passengers at each of the ten busiest airports in two consecutive years.

How to read it — Guwahati added the most in percentage terms (+7.5%); Kolkata changed -3.3%.

Why it matters — Shows which hubs are growing and which are flat.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise passenger traffic for the ten busiest airports.

indicators.title: Passenger Growth by Airport (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Change over 2024-25, top ten airports
indicators.details:
What it shows — Year-on-year change in passengers at the ten busiest airports.

How to read it — Guwahati grew fastest at +7.5%; Kolkata was weakest at -3.3%; Delhi changed -0.7%.

Why it matters — Separates fast-growing airports from mature or congested ones.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise passengers, percentage change computed from the two years.

indicators.title: Passengers by Airport Category
indicators.subtitle: 2024-25 vs 2025-26, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passengers handled by each AAI airport category: AAI international, PPP, JV, state/private, customs and domestic airports.

How to read it — JV international airports handled 224.7 million (53.5%); state/private international airports grew fastest (+22.9%).

Why it matters — Shows whether growth comes from the big JV hubs or from smaller airports.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure I: traffic by airport category.

indicators.title: Monthly Passengers: 2026 vs 2025
indicators.subtitle: January to September, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total monthly passengers at Indian airports, compared with the same month a year earlier.

How to read it — January 2026 was 38.63 million (+4.0% on a year earlier); by September it was 30.10 million (-5.9%).

Why it matters — Shows the seasonal pattern and whether growth is holding up.

series.note: AAI monthly Traffic News reports, January to September 2026 (month of 2026 against the same month of 2025), total passengers.

indicators.title: Monthly Passenger Growth, 2026
indicators.subtitle: Change on same month of 2025
indicators.details:
What it shows — Year-on-year change in total passengers for each month.

How to read it — Strongest month was May (+4.5%); weakest was Sep (-5.9%).

Why it matters — Reveals the turning point from growth to decline.

series.note: AAI monthly Traffic News reports, January to September 2026; percentage change computed from the reported monthly totals.

indicators.title: April-September 2026-27 vs 2025-26
indicators.subtitle: Cumulative change, passengers, freight and movements
indicators.details:
What it shows — Half-year change in passengers, air freight and aircraft movements.

How to read it — Freight is +11.7% while passengers are -2.9% and movements -3.5%.

Why it matters — Contrasts a cargo boom with softer passenger traffic.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, September 2026: cumulative April-September 2026-27 against April-September 2025-26 (passengers 196.24 vs 202.14 million; freight 2,192.38 vs 1,962.65 thousand tonnes; movements 1,377.29 vs 1,427.55 thousand).

indicators.title: Passengers at Indian Airports, 2018-19 to 2025-26
indicators.subtitle: Total domestic plus international, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total passengers handled at all Indian airports each financial year.

How to read it — From 344.7 million in 2018-19 to a low of 115.4 million in 2020-21, then 420.1 million in 2025-26.

Why it matters — The pandemic collapse and recovery in one series.

series.note: AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2022-23 (Board's Report, traffic at all Indian airports) for 2018-19 to 2022-23; AAI Annual Report 2023-24 for 2023-24; AAI Traffic News March 2026 for 2024-25 and 2025-26.

indicators.title: Yearly Passenger Growth, 2019-20 to 2025-26
indicators.subtitle: Change on previous financial year
indicators.details:
What it shows — Year-on-year growth in total airport passengers.

How to read it — Traffic fell -66.2% in 2020-21, rebounded +63.7% in 2021-22 and grew +1.9% in 2025-26.

Why it matters — Shows the size of the 2020-21 collapse and the 2021-22 rebound.

series.note: Computed from the total passengers series: AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2023-24 and AAI Traffic News March 2026.

indicators.title: Passengers per Aircraft Movement
indicators.subtitle: Average passengers on each takeoff or landing
indicators.details:
What it shows — Average passengers handled per aircraft movement across all airports (includes cargo and non-scheduled movements).

How to read it — 132 in 2018-19, 96 in 2020-21 and 145 in 2025-26.

Why it matters — Rising loads signal larger aircraft and fuller flights.

series.note: Computed: total passengers divided by total aircraft movements, from AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2023-24 and AAI Traffic News March 2026.

indicators.title: Passengers at AAI-Managed Airports, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.subtitle: Million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passengers at airports run by AAI itself, over eleven years.

How to read it — From 78.9 million in 2014-15 to 183.7 million in 2024-25, 2.3 times.

Why it matters — A long baseline showing growth at AAI's own network.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance (passenger movements at AAI airports; excludes JVC, state and private airports). Earlier years from AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 and 2020-21.

indicators.title: Aircraft Movements, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.subtitle: Thousand, all Indian airports
indicators.details:
What it shows — Takeoffs and landings at Indian airports over eleven years.

How to read it — From 1,603 thousand in 2014-15 to 2,887 thousand in 2024-25; the 2020-21 low was 1,197 thousand.

Why it matters — Movements are the flight-activity counterpart of passenger traffic.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance (aircraft movements); earlier years from AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 and 2020-21.

indicators.title: Air Passengers Carried by Indian Carriers
indicators.subtitle: Passengers on Indian-registered airlines
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passengers carried by air by carriers registered in India, domestic and international, in millions.

How to read it — From 10.9 in 1990 to 180.4 in 2023; the lowest point was 9.4 in 1993.

Why it matters — A long annual series shows how quickly Indian aviation has grown and how COVID-19 disrupted it.

datasets.label: Air Passengers Carried by Indian Carriers

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.PSGR, compiled from ICAO civil-aviation statistics for Indian-registered carriers.

indicators.title: Air Passengers: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: Passengers carried by registered carriers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air passengers carried by each country's airlines, in millions.

How to read it — India is the orange line; compare its trajectory with each peer.

Why it matters — Compares India's growth path with the largest aviation markets.

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.PSGR, compiled from ICAO civil-aviation statistics for carriers registered in each country. Gaps are years a country did not report.

indicators.title: Aircraft Departures: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: Departures by registered carriers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Take-offs by each country's registered carriers, in millions.

How to read it — India is the orange line; compare its trajectory with each peer.

Why it matters — Departures measure how often aircraft fly, not just how many people travel.

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.DPRT, compiled from ICAO civil-aviation statistics for carriers registered in each country. Gaps are years a country did not report.

indicators.title: Air Passengers per 100 People (2023)
indicators.subtitle: Passengers carried relative to population
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air passengers carried divided by population.

How to read it — India ranks 11 of 11 countries in this comparison.

Why it matters — Per-person figures show how far air travel has spread beyond big markets.

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.PSGR, 2023. India ranks 11 of 11 countries shown.

indicators.title: Passenger Recovery Index, 2019 = 100
indicators.subtitle: Registered-carrier passengers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passengers carried each year relative to 2019.

How to read it — India is at 107.7 in 2023; the orange line is India.

Why it matters — Shows how quickly each market recovered and then outgrew 2019.

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.PSGR: each country's passengers indexed to 2019 = 100, computed.

indicators.title: Growth in Passengers Carried by Indian Airlines
indicators.subtitle: Change on previous year
indicators.details:
What it shows — Annual percentage change in passengers carried by Indian carriers.

How to read it — Highest +66.7% in 2022; lowest -58.8% in 2020.

Why it matters — Shows the long-run growth rate and the pandemic shock.

datasets.label: Growth in Passengers Carried by Indian Airlines

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.PSGR: year-on-year change in passengers carried by Indian-registered carriers, computed.

indicators.title: Passenger Growth 2013-2023 (Annual Rate)
indicators.subtitle: Compound annual growth of passengers carried
indicators.details:
What it shows — Compound annual growth in passengers carried over ten years, including the pandemic.

How to read it — India grew 9.1% a year, rank 1 of 11.

Why it matters — Compares long-run growth across aviation markets.

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.PSGR: compound annual growth of passengers carried, 2013 to 2023, computed. India ranks 1 of 11.

indicators.title: Aircraft Departures by Indian Carriers
indicators.subtitle: Take-offs by Indian-registered airlines
indicators.details:
What it shows — Departures by carriers registered in India, in millions.

How to read it — From 0.1 in 1990 to 1.2 in 2023; the lowest point was 0.1 in 1993.

Why it matters — Departures track flight activity over time.

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.DPRT, compiled from ICAO civil-aviation statistics for Indian-registered carriers.

indicators.title: Operational Airports
indicators.subtitle: Airports, heliports and water aerodromes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Number of operational airports, heliports and water aerodromes.

How to read it — The count more than doubled from 74 in 2014 to 164 in 2025.

Why it matters — More airports bring air service to more districts.

series.note: Operational airports including heliports and water aerodromes: 74 in 2014 and 164 in 2025 (Ministry of Civil Aviation, Lok Sabha reply of 4 December 2025); 157 as at the date of the AAI Annual Report 2023-24 Board's Report (https://www.aai.aero/sites/default/files/AAI%20AR_2024_ENG_05.12.2024.pdf).

indicators.title: Airports Managed by AAI
indicators.subtitle: Operating model of AAI's 133 airports
indicators.details:
What it shows — How the 133 airports under AAI's management are operated.

How to read it — 125 are run directly by AAI, 6 by public-private partnerships and 2 by joint-venture companies (Delhi, Mumbai).

Why it matters — Shows how much of airport operations has moved to private operators.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Board's Report: AAI manages 133 airports, of which 8 are under private control: DIAL and MIAL as joint ventures and Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Guwahati, Thiruvananthapuram and Mangalore as PPPs.

indicators.title: UDAN Passengers Carried (Cumulative)
indicators.subtitle: Passengers on RCS-UDAN flights, lakh
indicators.details:
What it shows — Cumulative passengers carried on flights under the Regional Connectivity Scheme (UDAN).

How to read it — The total passed 159 lakh by December 2025, up from 117 lakh in March 2023.

Why it matters — Measures the reach of regional flying on subsidised routes.

series.note: Cumulative passengers carried under RCS-UDAN: 117 lakh up to 31 March 2023 and 136 lakh up to 31 March 2024 (Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24); more than 159 lakh as at 31 December 2025 (Ministry of Civil Aviation, https://www.civilaviation.gov.in/our-performance).

indicators.title: UDAN Routes Operationalised
indicators.subtitle: Cumulative RCS-UDAN routes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Cumulative routes started under the Regional Connectivity Scheme.

How to read it — Operational routes rose from 559 to 657 and the airports served from 84 to 93.

Why it matters — UDAN is the policy lever for small-city connectivity.

series.note: RCS-UDAN routes operationalised: 559 connecting 84 airports at 31 March 2024 (Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24); 657 routes and 93 airports at 31 December 2025 (Ministry of Civil Aviation, https://www.civilaviation.gov.in/our-performance).

indicators.title: UDAN Flights Operated (Cumulative)
indicators.subtitle: Flights under RCS-UDAN, lakh
indicators.details:
What it shows — Cumulative flights operated under UDAN.

How to read it — Flights rose from 2.24 lakh to about 3.34 lakh between March 2023 and December 2025.

Why it matters — Flights complement the passenger count to show service frequency.

series.note: Cumulative RCS-UDAN flights operated: 2.24 lakh up to 31 March 2023 and 2.62 lakh up to 31 March 2024 (Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24); about 3.34 lakh at 31 December 2025 (Ministry of Civil Aviation, https://www.civilaviation.gov.in/our-performance).

indicators.title: Busiest Airports by Aircraft Movements (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Takeoffs and landings, thousand
indicators.details:
What it shows — Aircraft movements at the ten busiest Indian airports.

How to read it — Delhi leads at 473.5 thousand (25.1% of the 10 shown); Guwahati is lowest at 47.4 thousand.

Why it matters — Movements show runway load, the binding constraint at hubs.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise aircraft movements.

indicators.title: Passengers by Airport Category (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Share of 420.09 million passengers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Which kinds of airport handle India's passengers.

How to read it — JV international airports handle 53.5%; domestic and state-run domestic airports together only 6.5%.

Why it matters — Private JV hubs dominate traffic while most airports are small.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure I: traffic by airport category.

indicators.title: Aircraft Movements by Airport Category
indicators.subtitle: 2024-25 vs 2025-26, thousand
indicators.details:
What it shows — Takeoffs and landings by airport category.

How to read it — JV international airports had 1,400 thousand movements (+1.7%).

Why it matters — Shows where flying activity is growing.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure I: aircraft movements by airport category.

indicators.title: Passengers by AAI Region (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Share of 420.09 million passengers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Passenger traffic by AAI region.

How to read it — Southern region handles 32.6% and Northern 28.1%; North East 2.9%.

Why it matters — Shows the regional balance of air travel.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure V: region-wise traffic.

indicators.title: Aircraft Movement Growth by Region (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Change on 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — Change in aircraft movements by AAI region.

How to read it — Eastern grew +3.8% while Northern changed -3.0% and North East -1.6%.

Why it matters — Shows which regions are adding flight activity.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure V: region-wise aircraft movements; percentage change computed.

indicators.title: Passengers by State (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Top ten states, million
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total passengers at airports in each state.

How to read it — Delhi leads with 78.7 million; the top ten states handle 83.7% of national passengers.

Why it matters — Shows which states generate the most air travel.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure VI: state-wise traffic (domestic plus international).

indicators.title: Top Five Airports' Share of Passengers (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Share of 420.09 million passengers
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much of India's traffic the five busiest airports carry.

How to read it — The top five handle 55.2% of passengers; 140 other airports share the rest.

Why it matters — Concentration drives the case for new airports.

datasets.label: Top Five Airports' Share of Passengers (2025-26)

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise passengers against the all-India total of 420,089,356.

indicators.title: UDAN Expenditure by Year
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, Phase-I and Phase-II
indicators.details:
What it shows — Money spent each year on reviving airports and heliports under UDAN.

How to read it — Spending peaked at Rs 800.92 crore in 2022-23; cumulative expenditure is Rs 4,071.98 crore.

Why it matters — Shows the pace of regional airport investment.

series.note: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 2858 (8 August 2024), Ministry of Civil Aviation, Annexure: budget allocated and utilised under UDAN. Phase-I allocation Rs 4,500 crore, Phase-II Rs 1,000 crore.

indicators.title: UDAN Viability Gap Funding by Year
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore disbursed to airlines
indicators.details:
What it shows — Subsidy paid to airlines to operate regional routes.

How to read it — Rs 787.37 crore was disbursed in 2022-23, the peak; the total to July 2024 is Rs 3,512.29 crore.

Why it matters — VGF is the main running cost of the regional connectivity scheme.

datasets.label: UDAN Viability Gap Funding by Year

series.note: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 2858: VGF disbursed in RACFT from 2017 to 31 July 2024; 2023-24 is provisional, 2024-25 covers April-July.

indicators.title: UDAN Routes: Awarded, Operational, Discontinued
indicators.subtitle: As on 8 August 2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Status of routes awarded under the Regional Connectivity Scheme.

How to read it — 66.6% of awarded routes are operational; 106 routes were discontinued early.

Why it matters — Many awarded routes never start or end early.

series.note: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 2858: 870 valid routes awarded, 579 operationalised connecting 85 airports (13 heliports, 2 water aerodromes); 106 discontinued before the three-year tenure ended.

indicators.title: AAI Operational Airports by Type
indicators.subtitle: Annual Report 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — Number of airports AAI operates and how many are civil enclaves, international or privately run.

How to read it — Of 113 operational AAI airports, 38 handle international flights, 29 are civil enclaves in defence airfields and 8 are privately operated.

Why it matters — Shows the structure of AAI's network.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Corporate overview, Operational AAI Airports (113 total; 29 civil enclaves, 38 with international operations and 8 under private control are out of the 113).

indicators.title: Air Freight: Domestic vs International
indicators.subtitle: Freight handled, thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air freight handled at all Indian airports.

How to read it — Total freight grew 7.0% to 3,365.68 thousand tonnes; international freight grew 9.7% and domestic 3.0%.

Why it matters — Air cargo carries high-value goods and links India to world trade.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Board's Report, freight handled at all Indian airports.

indicators.title: Air Freight Mix (2023-24)
indicators.subtitle: Share of 3,365.68 thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — International and domestic share of air freight in 2023-24.

How to read it — International freight is 60.8% and domestic 39.2%, the reverse of passenger traffic.

Why it matters — Cargo is more export-driven than passenger flying.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Board's Report, 2023-24 freight at all Indian airports.

indicators.title: Air Cargo Handled Over a Decade
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air cargo handled at Indian airports.

How to read it — Cargo rose from 2.53 million tonnes in 2014-15 to 3.72 million tonnes in 2024-25, up 47%.

Why it matters — A ten-year view shows structural growth beyond the COVID-19 swing.

datasets.label: Air Cargo Handled Over a Decade

series.note: Air cargo handled: 2.53 million tonnes in 2014-15 and 3.72 million tonnes in 2024-25 (Ministry of Civil Aviation, https://www.civilaviation.gov.in/our-performance); 3.37 million tonnes (3,365.68 thousand) in 2023-24 from the AAI Annual Report.

indicators.title: Busiest Airports by Freight (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air freight handled at the ten busiest cargo airports.

How to read it — Delhi handled 1,148 thousand tonnes and Mumbai 927: together 52.4% of national freight.

Why it matters — Cargo is even more concentrated than passenger traffic.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise freight (domestic plus international).

indicators.title: Airport Freight: 2024-25 vs 2025-26
indicators.subtitle: Thousand tonnes, top ten airports
indicators.details:
What it shows — Freight at each of the ten busiest cargo airports in two years.

How to read it — Pune grew +29.4% and Chennai +11.4%; Delhi +3.5%.

Why it matters — Shows which cargo hubs are expanding.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise freight.

indicators.title: Freight Growth by Airport (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Change on 2024-25, top ten airports
indicators.details:
What it shows — Year-on-year change in freight at the ten busiest cargo airports.

How to read it — Fastest: Pune +29.4%; slowest: Kolkata +1.6%.

Why it matters — Highlights fast-rising cargo airports.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): percentage change computed from airport-wise freight.

indicators.title: International Freight by Airport (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — International air freight at the ten leading gateways.

How to read it — Delhi 740, Mumbai 695, Bengaluru and Chennai lead; the top four are 85.7% of India's international freight.

Why it matters — Most export and import cargo moves through four airports.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure IV: international freight by airport.

indicators.title: Freight by Airport Category (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Share of 3.96 million tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Which airport categories carry India's air freight.

How to read it — JV international airports handle 72.4% of freight.

Why it matters — Cargo is overwhelmingly handled by the JV hubs.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure I: freight by airport category.

indicators.title: Freight by AAI Region
indicators.subtitle: 2024-25 vs 2025-26, thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air freight in each AAI region.

How to read it — Southern 1,281 thousand tonnes (+7.8%) and Northern 1,239 (+3.9%) lead.

Why it matters — Shows regional cargo capacity.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure V: region-wise freight.

indicators.title: Freight by State (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Top ten states, thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air freight handled in each state.

How to read it — Delhi 1,148 and Maharashtra 1,003 thousand tonnes lead the table.

Why it matters — Shows where cargo flows concentrate.

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25), Annexure VI: state-wise freight.

indicators.title: Air Freight at Indian Airports, 2018-19 to 2025-26
indicators.subtitle: Thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — International and domestic air freight by financial year.

How to read it — Total freight dipped to 2,474 thousand tonnes in 2020-21 and reached 3,964 thousand tonnes in 2025-26, +11.3% against 2018-19.

Why it matters — Cargo held up far better than passengers during the pandemic.

series.note: AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2023-24 (Board's Report) and AAI Traffic News March 2026, freight at all Indian airports.

indicators.title: Yearly Freight Growth, 2019-20 to 2025-26
indicators.subtitle: Change on previous financial year
indicators.details:
What it shows — Year-on-year growth in air freight.

How to read it — Freight fell -25.7% in 2020-21, rose +27.0% in 2021-22 and +6.2% in 2025-26.

Why it matters — Shows the cargo cycle through the pandemic.

series.note: Computed from total freight: AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2023-24 and AAI Traffic News March 2026.

indicators.title: International Share of Air Freight
indicators.subtitle: % of all freight
indicators.details:
What it shows — International freight as a share of all freight handled.

How to read it — 61.8% in 2018-19 and 61.8% in 2025-26.

Why it matters — International cargo is the bigger part of Indian air freight.

series.note: Computed from international and total freight: AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2023-24 and AAI Traffic News March 2026.

indicators.title: Cargo at AAI Airports, 2014-15 to 2019-20
indicators.subtitle: Thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Cargo handled at airports operated by AAI.

How to read it — Rose from 681 to 942 thousand tonnes by 2018-19, then eased to 910.

Why it matters — A pre-pandemic baseline for cargo at AAI's own network.

series.note: AAI Annual Report 2019-20 and 2020-21, Performance at a Glance: cargo handled at AAI airports (later reports stop reporting this line).

indicators.title: Monthly Air Freight: 2026 vs 2025
indicators.subtitle: January to September, thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total air freight handled each month.

How to read it — September 2026 freight was 372.3 thousand tonnes, +12.1% on a year earlier.

Why it matters — Shows whether the cargo boom is persistent.

series.note: AAI monthly Traffic News reports, January to September 2026 against the same months of 2025, total freight.

indicators.title: Monthly Freight: International vs Domestic
indicators.subtitle: 2026, thousand tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — International and domestic freight each month of 2026.

How to read it — International freight rose from 201 thousand tonnes in January to 243 in September.

Why it matters — International freight is growing the fastest.

series.note: AAI monthly Traffic News reports, January to September 2026.

indicators.title: Top Five Airports' Share of Freight (2025-26)
indicators.subtitle: Share of 3.96 million tonnes
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much of India's freight the five busiest cargo airports carry.

How to read it — The top five handle 81.0% of freight.

Why it matters — Cargo capacity is concentrated.

datasets.label: Top Five Airports' Share of Freight (2025-26)

series.note: AAI Traffic News, March 2026 report and annexures (April-March 2025-26 against 2024-25): airport-wise freight against the national total of 3,964,346.6 tonnes.

indicators.title: Air Freight: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: Freight carried by registered carriers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air freight in million tonne-kilometres.

How to read it — India is the orange line; compare its trajectory with each peer.

Why it matters — Air freight tracks high-value trade.

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.GOOD.MT.K1, compiled from ICAO civil-aviation statistics for carriers registered in each country. Gaps are years a country did not report.

indicators.title: Air Freight Ranking (2023)
indicators.subtitle: Freight carried by registered carriers
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air freight in million tonne-kilometres.

How to read it — India ranks 8 of 11 countries in this comparison.

Why it matters — Ranks India's air cargo output.

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.GOOD.MT.K1, 2023. India ranks 8 of 11 countries shown.

indicators.title: Share of Air Freight Among Peers (2023)
indicators.subtitle: Peer share of air freight
indicators.details:
What it shows — Each country's share of the peer group's air freight.

How to read it — India ranks 8 of 11 countries in this comparison.

Why it matters — Shows India's weight in global air cargo.

datasets.label: Share of Air Freight Among Peers (2023)

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.GOOD.MT.K1, 2023. India ranks 8 of 11 countries shown.

indicators.title: India's Share of World Air Freight
indicators.subtitle: India as % of the world total
indicators.details:
What it shows — India's air freight (tonne-km) as a percentage of the world total.

How to read it — 1.18% in 1990, a peak of 1.22% in 2018 and 0.84% in 2023.

Why it matters — Shows India's weight in global air cargo.

datasets.label: India's Share of World Air Freight

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.GOOD.MT.K1 (ICAO data): India's value divided by the world aggregate (WLD), computed for each year both are reported.

indicators.title: Air Freight by Indian Carriers
indicators.subtitle: Million tonne-km
indicators.details:
What it shows — Air freight carried by Indian-registered carriers in million tonne-kilometres.

How to read it — From 0.0 in 1990 to 0.0 in 2023; the lowest point was 0.0 in 1991.

Why it matters — A long run of Indian air-cargo output.

series.note: World Bank indicator IS.AIR.GOOD.MT.K1, compiled from ICAO civil-aviation statistics for Indian-registered carriers.

indicators.title: AAI Revenue and Profit
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, 2018-19 to 2023-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — Revenue and profit of the Airports Authority of India.

How to read it — Revenue fell to Rs 4,867 crore and AAI lost Rs 1,962 crore after tax in 2020-21; in 2023-24 revenue was Rs 15,980 crore and profit after tax Rs 4,651 crore.

Why it matters — AAI's finances track air traffic closely.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Performance at a Glance, income and profit.

indicators.title: AAI Capital Expenditure vs Plan
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, 2018-19 to 2023-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — AAI's planned and actual capital expenditure.

How to read it — Actual spend was Rs 5,335 crore in 2023-24 against a plan outlay of Rs 4,000 crore.

Why it matters — Capital expenditure builds terminals, runways and air navigation capacity.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2023-24: Performance at a Glance, annual plan outlay and actual capital expenditure.

indicators.title: AAI Income and Profit, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore
indicators.details:
What it shows — AAI revenue, expenditure and profit over eleven years.

How to read it — Revenue reached Rs 20,648 crore and profit after tax Rs 7,233 crore in 2024-25; 2020-21 was a Rs 1,962 crore loss.

Why it matters — Shows the pandemic loss and the record profits since.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance; earlier years from AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 and 2020-21. Revenue less expenditure equals profit before tax in every year.

indicators.title: AAI Pre-Tax Profit Margin
indicators.subtitle: Profit before tax as % of revenue
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much of each rupee of revenue turns into pre-tax profit.

How to read it — Margin was 30.1% in 2014-15, -56.9% in 2020-21 and 46.8% in 2024-25.

Why it matters — Margin shows efficiency beyond raw growth.

series.note: Computed from revenue and profit before tax, Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance (and AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 and 2020-21).

indicators.title: AAI Capital Expenditure, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, actual spend
indicators.details:
What it shows — AAI's actual capital expenditure every year.

How to read it — Spending rose from Rs 1,400 crore to a record Rs 5,569 crore, 4.0 times.

Why it matters — Capital expenditure builds terminals, runways and air navigation capacity.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance and Board's Report (capital expenditure Rs 5,568.55 crore in 2024-25); earlier years from AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 and 2020-21.

indicators.title: How AAI Funds Its Capital Expenditure
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore by source, 2018-19 to 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — Capital expenditure split by internal resources, grants, budget support and borrowing.

How to read it — Internal resources funded Rs 5,151 crore in 2024-25; commercial borrowings were used in 2020-21 to 2022-23.

Why it matters — Shows how reliant AAI is on its own cash.

series.note: AAI Annual Reports 2018-19 to 2024-25 (Board's Report, capital expenditure by source of funds). Sources sum to total actual capital expenditure in each year.

indicators.title: Capex Funding Mix (2021-22)
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore by source
indicators.details:
What it shows — Sources of AAI's capital spending in 2021-22.

How to read it — Commercial borrowings funded 34.3% against 16.3% from internal resources.

Why it matters — A pandemic year when internal resources fell and borrowing rose.

series.note: AAI Annual Report 2021-22 (Board's Report): capital expenditure by source of funds, total Rs 3,724.34 crore.

indicators.title: AAI Employees, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.subtitle: Number of employees
indicators.details:
What it shows — AAI's workforce.

How to read it — Staff 17,465 in 2014-15 and 16,251 in 2024-25 while movements rose 80%.

Why it matters — Traffic has grown far faster than the workforce.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance (employees); earlier years from AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 and 2020-21.

indicators.title: Aircraft Movements per AAI Employee
indicators.subtitle: Productivity, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — Annual movements handled per AAI employee.

How to read it — 92 in 2014-15, 71 in 2020-21 and 178 in 2024-25.

Why it matters — A simple productivity measure.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance (aircraft movements per employee).

indicators.title: AAI Revenue per Employee
indicators.subtitle: Rs thousand, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — Annual AAI revenue per employee.

How to read it — Rs 5,325 thousand in 2014-15 rising to Rs 12,706 thousand in 2024-25.

Why it matters — Shows financial productivity.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance (revenue per employee).

indicators.title: AAI Net Worth and Capital Work-in-Progress
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — AAI's net worth and projects still under construction.

How to read it — Net worth reached Rs 23,981 crore in 2024-25, up from Rs 11,417 crore.

Why it matters — Net worth shows financial strength; work-in-progress shows pending projects.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance (net worth, capital WIP); earlier years from AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 and 2020-21.

indicators.title: AAI Dividend Paid, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, including interim dividend
indicators.details:
What it shows — Dividend AAI paid to the Government of India.

How to read it — Dividend reached Rs 2,170 crore in 2024-25, with none in 2020-21 and 2021-22.

Why it matters — Dividends are the Government's direct return from AAI.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Performance at a Glance (dividend including interim). The report shows no dividend ('-') in 2020-21 and 2021-22, plotted as zero.

indicators.title: AAI Borrowings (Loans from Others)
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, 2014-15 to 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — Loans AAI has outstanding from lenders other than the Government.

How to read it — Peaked at Rs 3,152 crore in 2021-22 and stood at Rs 2,171 crore in 2024-25.

indicators.title: AAI Revenue by Source, 2018-19 to 2022-23

indicators.details:

How to read it — Air navigation services earned Rs 3,550 crore in 2022-23; JVC lease Rs 3,021 crore.

Why it matters — Shows how AAI earns its money and how it depends on lease income.

series.note: AAI Annual Report 2022-23 (Board's Report, income analysis) and earlier reports; components sum to total revenue within rounding.

indicators.title: AAI Revenue Mix (2022-23)
indicators.subtitle: Share of Rs 12,172 crore
indicators.details:
What it shows — Where AAI's 2022-23 revenue came from.

How to read it — Air navigation is 29.2% and JVC lease 24.8% of revenue.

Why it matters — A quarter of revenue is lease income from private airports.

series.note: AAI Annual Report 2022-23: income analysis; components sum to total revenue Rs 12,172.35 crore.

indicators.title: AAI Non-Aeronautical Revenue
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, 2018-19 to 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — Revenue from retail, parking, advertising and rentals at airports.

How to read it — Rs 1,911 crore in 2024-25, 1.04 times 2018-19.

Why it matters — Commercial income reduces reliance on aeronautical charges.

series.note: AAI Annual Reports 2018-19 to 2022-23 (income analysis) and Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25 (non-aeronautical revenue).

indicators.title: AAI PPP Airport Concession Fees
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, 2020-21 to 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — Fees AAI receives from the six leased PPP airports.

How to read it — Rs 87 crore in 2020-21 to Rs 3,193 crore in 2024-25, boosted by the one-off recovery.

Why it matters — Shows how privatised airports feed AAI revenue.

series.note: AAI Annual Reports 2020-21 to 2022-23 and Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25 (revenue from PPP airports). The 2024-25 figure includes a one-time Rs 2,231.80 crore under-recovery from six PPP airports.

indicators.title: AAI Operating Revenue vs Other Income
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, 2019-20 to 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — AAI's operating revenue and other income.

How to read it — Operating revenue Rs 19,473 crore and other income Rs 1,176 crore in 2024-25.

Why it matters — Most income is from operations.

series.note: AAI Annual Reports 2019-20 to 2024-25 (statement of profit and loss, Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25).

indicators.title: AAI Cost Structure
indicators.subtitle: Rs crore, 2023-24 and 2024-25
indicators.details:
What it shows — AAI's expenditure split into operating costs, finance costs and depreciation.

How to read it — Operating costs are 72.9% of 2024-25 expenditure; depreciation rose 9.5%.

Why it matters — Shows how costs grow with capital investment.

series.note: Airports Authority of India, Annual Report 2024-25: Board's Report, expenditure analysis; the three heads sum to total expenditure (Rs 9,765.83 crore in 2023-24, Rs 10,992.79 crore in 2024-25).

indicators.title: Cargo Handled by Major Port (2023-24)
indicators.subtitle: Ranked port throughput; provisional values
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total cargo handled at each of the 13 major ports in 2023-24.

How to read it — Deendayal handled 132.374 million tonnes; Kolkata handled 16.856 million tonnes.

Why it matters — Shows where major-port freight activity is concentrated.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Performance of Major Ports’, printed p.51; provisional 2023-24.

indicators.title: Major Port Cargo: Year-on-Year
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes by port
indicators.details:

How to read it — The 13 port values sum to 819.227 million tonnes in 2023-24.

Why it matters — Compares port-level traffic year over year.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Performance of Major Ports’, printed p.51; 2022-23 actual and 2023-24 provisional.

indicators.title: Major-Port Cargo Share by Port
indicators.subtitle: 2023-24 composition
indicators.details:
What it shows — Each port's contribution to major-port cargo.

How to read it — Port values sum to 819.227 million tonnes.

Why it matters — Shows relative contribution of each major port.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Performance of Major Ports’, printed p.51; 2023-24 provisional values; shares are within the 13 listed ports.

indicators.title: Major-Port Cargo Throughput
indicators.subtitle: All major ports, 2017-18 to 2023-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — Annual total cargo handled at major ports.

How to read it — Throughput reached 819.23 MMT in 2023-24, up from 784.31 MMT.

Why it matters — Puts the latest year in long-run context.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16.

indicators.title: Major and Non-Major Port Cargo
indicators.subtitle: All-port, major-port and derived residuals
indicators.details:
What it shows — All-port traffic and reported major-port totals; non-major values are residuals.

How to read it — Derived non-major traffic is 649.88 MMT in 2022-23 and approximately 720.77 MMT in 2023-24; the latter inherits rounding from 1,540 MMT.

Why it matters — Separates the major-port system without presenting the residual as a directly reported statistic.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.11, ‘Cargo Traffic at Indian Ports’, printed p.16; non-major values are derived as all-port less major-port traffic; 2023-24 all-port traffic is approximate 1,540 MMT.

indicators.title: Major vs Non-Major Port Share
indicators.subtitle: Approximate 2023-24 composition
indicators.details:
What it shows — Reported major-port cargo and a derived non-major-port residual.

How to read it — Approximately 819.23 MMT major and 720.77 MMT non-major; the latter is derived from rounded all-port data.

Why it matters — Shows a transparent estimate of cargo distribution across port categories.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.11, printed p.16; non-major ports = approximate 1,540 MMT all-port total less 819.23 MMT major-port total.

indicators.title: Major-Port Cargo by Commodity

How to read it — 2023-24 totals: POL 245.99 MMT, coal 191.98 MMT, containerised cargo 181.57 MMT.

Why it matters — Shows how port freight composition changes over time.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16.

indicators.title: Major-Port Commodity Mix (2023-24)
indicators.subtitle: Share of reported 819.23 MMT

How to read it — The six groups sum to 819.23 MMT.

Why it matters — Compares the latest commodity composition.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16. 2023-24 column.

indicators.title: POL at Major Ports
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes, 2017-18 to 2023-24
indicators.details:

How to read it — POL reached 245.99 MMT in 2023-24. POL includes crude, products and LPG/LNG.

Why it matters — Tracks this freight stream over time.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16.

indicators.title: Coal Cargo at Major Ports
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes, 2017-18 to 2023-24
indicators.details:

Why it matters — Tracks this freight stream over time.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16.

indicators.title: Iron Ore Cargo at Major Ports
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes, 2017-18 to 2023-24
indicators.details:

Why it matters — Tracks this freight stream over time.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16.

indicators.title: Fertilisers and Raw Materials at Major Ports
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes, 2017-18 to 2023-24
indicators.details:

Why it matters — Tracks this freight stream over time.

datasets.label: Fertilisers and Raw Materials at Major Ports

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16.

indicators.title: Containerised Cargo at Major Ports
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes, 2017-18 to 2023-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — Major-port cargo volume for Containerised cargo.

How to read it — Containerised cargo reached 181.57 MMT in 2023-24. Cargo weight is in million tonnes; TEUs are charted separately.

Why it matters — Tracks this freight stream over time.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16.

indicators.title: Other Cargo at Major Ports

Why it matters — Tracks this freight stream over time.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16.

indicators.title: Major-Port Container Throughput

Why it matters — TEUs measure container traffic independently of container cargo weight.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, §2.12 and Table ‘Commodity-wise Cargo Traffic at Major Ports’, printed p.16.

indicators.title: Major-Port Capacity vs Traffic

Why it matters — Shows installed capacity relative to freight volume.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Capacity at Major Ports’, printed p.52; 2016-17 uses reported capacity, excluding the separately footnoted re-rated figure.

indicators.title: Major-Port Capacity Utilisation
indicators.subtitle: Traffic as a share of rated capacity
indicators.details:
What it shows — Annual major-port traffic divided by rated capacity.

How to read it — Calculated utilisation was 50.26% in 2023-24.

Why it matters — A derived ratio compares actual throughput with rated capacity.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Capacity at Major Ports’, printed p.52; ratio calculated as traffic / capacity × 100.

indicators.title: Average Vessel Turnaround by Major Port
indicators.subtitle: 2023-24 provisional
indicators.details:
What it shows — Average vessel turnaround time for each major port.

How to read it — Jawaharlal Nehru recorded 26.00 hours; Kolkata 82.61; all-ports average 48.06.

Why it matters — Measures vessel time in port from pilot boarding to deboarding.

datasets.label: Average Vessel Turnaround by Major Port

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Average Turn Round Time’, printed p.52; 2023-24 provisional; time measured from pilot boarding to deboarding.

indicators.title: Average Vessel Turnaround Time
indicators.subtitle: All major ports, 2022-23 to 2023-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — Average vessel turnaround at all major ports.

How to read it — The average fell from 52.90 to 48.06 hours.

Why it matters — Lower turnaround means less time spent by vessels in port.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Average Turn Round Time’, printed pp.52-53; all-ports total, 2023-24 provisional.

indicators.title: Container-Ship Turnaround Time
indicators.subtitle: Major sea ports, 2022-23 to 2023-24
indicators.details:

How to read it — Container ship turnaround was 30.10 and 30.12 hours.

Why it matters — Separates container-vessel turnaround from the all-vessel average.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Average Turn Round Time’, printed p.53; container ships.

indicators.title: Cargo Output per Ship Berth Day by Port
indicators.subtitle: 2023-24 provisional
indicators.details:

Why it matters — Normalizes cargo-handling productivity by vessel berth time.

datasets.label: Cargo Output per Ship Berth Day by Port

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Average Output per Ship Berth Day’, printed p.53; 2023-24 provisional.

indicators.title: Average Output per Ship Berth Day
indicators.subtitle: All major ports, 2022-23 to 2023-24
indicators.details:
What it shows — Average cargo output per ship berth day.

How to read it — The all-ports average rose from 17,605 to 18,925 tonnes.

Why it matters — Higher output indicates greater average cargo-handling productivity.

datasets.label: Average Output per Ship Berth Day

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Table ‘Average Output per Ship Berth Day’, printed p.53; all-ports total.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Score Card—Inland Waterways, printed p.3; values are rounded; overview reports 133 MMTPA.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Score Card—Inland Waterways, printed p.3; Operational NWs for river cruise.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Score Card—Inland Waterways, printed p.3; derived index with 2022-23 as base.

series.note: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Annual Report 2023-24, Score Card—Ports, printed p.3; Coastal Cargo Handled (MMTPA).
