indicators.title: CO2 Emissions per Person
indicators.subtitle: Tonnes of CO2 per capita, excluding land use
indicators.details:
What it shows — Carbon dioxide released per Indian each year from fossil fuels, cement and industry.

How to read it — A rising line means emissions are growing faster than population. India's figure is about a third of the world average and a sixth of the US level.

Why it matters — Per-person emissions frame India's climate-equity argument: total emissions are large, but each citizen's footprint is small.

series.note: Tonnes of CO2 per capita, excluding land use. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator EN.GHG.CO2.PC.CE.AR5); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Total Greenhouse Gas Emissions
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes of CO2-equivalent, excluding land use
indicators.details:
What it shows — All greenhouse gases India emits each year (CO2, methane, nitrous oxide and F-gases), converted to CO2-equivalent.

How to read it — The slope shows how fast emissions are growing; compare it with GDP growth to judge whether the economy is decarbonising.

Why it matters — India is now the world's third-largest emitter in total, which makes its 2070 net-zero pathway globally significant.

series.note: Million tonnes of CO2-equivalent, excluding land use. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator EN.GHG.ALL.MT.CE.AR5); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Protected Areas
indicators.subtitle: Terrestrial and marine protected areas, % of territory
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of India's land and territorial waters inside national parks, sanctuaries and other protected areas.

How to read it — Higher is more protected; the global 30x30 target asks countries to protect 30% by 2030.

Why it matters — Protected areas safeguard tigers, elephants and watersheds, but expanding them must be balanced against forest-dwellers' rights.

series.note: Terrestrial and marine protected areas, % of territory. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator ER.PTD.TOTL.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Renewable Freshwater per Person
indicators.subtitle: Cubic metres of internal renewable water per person
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much renewable freshwater (rivers and groundwater recharge) India has per person.

How to read it — The total resource is roughly fixed, so the line falls as population grows. Below 1,700 m3 a country is 'water-stressed'; below 1,000 it is 'water-scarce'.

Why it matters — Falling water per person explains groundwater depletion, inter-State river disputes and the push for micro-irrigation and Jal Jeevan Mission.

series.note: Cubic metres of internal renewable water per person. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator ER.H2O.INTR.PC); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Population Density
indicators.subtitle: People per square kilometre of land
indicators.details:
What it shows — The average number of people living on each square kilometre of India's land.

How to read it — A steadily rising line; India is one of the most densely populated large countries.

Why it matters — Density raises pressure on land, forests, water and cities, and shapes disaster exposure.

series.note: People per square kilometre of land. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator EN.POP.DNST); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: All-India Mean Temperature by Season
indicators.subtitle: Area-weighted average temperature, °C (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — The India Meteorological Department's all-India average air temperature for the whole year and for each season, from 2001.

How to read it — Each line is one season. A line that drifts upward over the years means that season is getting warmer; compare the annual line with the pre-monsoon line to see where heat is concentrated.

Why it matters — Rising temperatures drive heat stress, crop losses, power demand and water scarcity, so this is the baseline for every climate-adaptation discussion.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 1 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: All-India Annual Rainfall
indicators.subtitle: Sum of monthly all-India rainfall, mm (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total rainfall received across India in each calendar year, built by adding the IMD's twelve monthly all-India averages.

How to read it — Taller bars are wetter years. Look for short bars: they usually line up with drought years and weak monsoons, such as 2002, 2009 and 2014-15.

Why it matters — Roughly half of India's farmland is rain-fed, so a poor rainfall year shows up quickly in farm output, rural incomes, food prices and reservoir levels.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 3 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Southwest Monsoon Rainfall (June-September)
indicators.subtitle: Sum of June-September all-India rainfall, mm (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Rain delivered by the southwest monsoon, the four months from June to September, in each year.

How to read it — Compare each bar with the others: the monsoon normally brings about three-quarters of India's annual rain, so dips here explain most dry years in the annual chart.

Why it matters — Kharif sowing, groundwater recharge, hydropower and rural demand all depend on the monsoon; the RBI and the Finance Ministry track it closely for inflation and growth.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 3 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Cyclonic Storms over the North Indian Ocean
indicators.subtitle: Storms formed in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea per year (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — The number of cyclonic storms that formed each year over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea, as recorded by the IMD.

How to read it — Each bar counts storms, not damage. Year-to-year swings are natural; look at decades together to judge whether storms are becoming more frequent.

Why it matters — Cyclones threaten a coastline that is home to millions of people. Better forecasting and evacuation have cut deaths sharply even when storm counts have not fallen.

datasets.label: Cyclonic Storms over the North Indian Ocean

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 89 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Heat Wave Days by State (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Average heat wave days in the summer season (IMD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — How many heat wave days each State recorded in the most recent summer season, as declared by the IMD.

How to read it — Longer bars mean more days of dangerous heat. Northern and central plains usually top the list.

Why it matters — Heat waves kill outdoor workers, the elderly and the poor, cut labour productivity and stress power grids; State heat-action plans target the worst-hit regions.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 87 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2024. Ranked highest to lowest.

indicators.title: India's Forest Cover
indicators.subtitle: Total forest cover, sq km (Forest Survey of India)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total area under forest cover in India from each State of Forest Report, built from satellite mapping by the Forest Survey of India.

How to read it — Each point is one biennial assessment; a rising line means more mapped forest cover. Mapping methods and resolution have improved over time, so small changes are within error.

Why it matters — Forests store carbon, protect watersheds and support tribal livelihoods; India's climate pledge includes adding a carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes through forests and tree cover.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 20 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). The source files the national total under a State label in some years; it is detected and used as the all-India value.

indicators.title: Forest Cover by State (2023)
indicators.subtitle: Forest cover in the latest State of Forest Report, sq km
indicators.details:
What it shows — The forest area of each State and UT in the most recent State of Forest Report.

How to read it — Bars are absolute areas, so large States lead. Madhya Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Odisha usually hold the biggest forests.

Why it matters — Forest-rich States carry much of India's carbon sink and biodiversity; forest area is also one factor in how the Finance Commission shares central taxes with States.

labels: Daman and Diu and Dadra Nagar Haveli
series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 20 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2023. Ranked highest to lowest.

indicators.title: Deaths from Forces of Nature by Cause (2022)
indicators.subtitle: Share of accidental deaths due to natural causes (NCRB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — How deaths attributed to forces of nature in the latest year split by cause, from NCRB's Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India.

How to read it — Bigger slices are bigger killers. Lightning is usually the largest single cause, ahead of floods and heat stroke.

Why it matters — Lightning and heat kill more people than dramatic disasters such as earthquakes, which points disaster-risk spending toward early warnings and shelters.

datasets.label: Deaths from Forces of Nature by Cause (2022)

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 94 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2022.

indicators.title: Deaths from Forces of Nature
indicators.subtitle: Total accidental deaths due to natural causes (NCRB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — The total number of people killed by natural causes (lightning, floods, heat, cold, landslides, storms and others) each year.

How to read it — Each bar is one year. Spikes usually match a severe flood, cyclone or heat season.

Why it matters — This tracks the human cost of climate and weather extremes, and whether early-warning systems are saving lives.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 94 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Electricity Generation by Source (2023-24)
indicators.subtitle: Share of gross generation, GWh (CEA)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Where India's electricity came from in the latest year, by fuel, from Central Electricity Authority data.

How to read it — Each slice is a share of total generation. Coal still dominates; the renewables slice (solar, wind, small hydro, biomass) is the one to watch.

Why it matters — India has pledged 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070, so the coal-to-renewables balance is the core energy-transition metric.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 41 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2023-24.

indicators.title: Electricity Generation since Independence
indicators.subtitle: Gross generation by source, GWh (CEA)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Gross electricity generated in India by source from 1947 to the latest year.

How to read it — Lines show absolute output, so thermal power's steep climb shows how India electrified. Renewables appear only from the 2000s and are now rising fastest.

Why it matters — Electricity use tracks industrialisation and living standards; the mix shows how carbon-intensive that growth has been.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 41 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Freshwater Withdrawals
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2022
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total annual freshwater withdrawals for agriculture, industry and households. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 647.5 bn cubic metres in 2022. Bigger slices show countries pulling most water from rivers and aquifers.

Why it matters — India is among the largest water users globally.

series.note: Freshwater Withdrawals: India's annual series, 1980 to 2022; the latest value is 647.5 bn cubic metres. Source: World Bank API ER.H2O.FWTL.K3 (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.details:

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2022; India ranks 1 of 15 (1 = highest value). Bigger slices show countries pulling most water from rivers and aquifers.

Why it matters — India is among the largest water users globally.

series.note: Freshwater Withdrawals, 2022: India ranks 1 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API ER.H2O.FWTL.K3 (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Freshwater Withdrawals: Share Among Peers (2022)
indicators.subtitle: Each country's share of the 15-country total
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total annual freshwater withdrawals for agriculture, industry and households. Slices show each country's share of the sampled countries' total.

How to read it — Slices are shares of the group total in 2022; India holds 26.8% and ranks 1 of 15. A bigger slice means a larger absolute amount, not a better outcome.

Why it matters — India is among the largest water users globally.

series.note: Freshwater Withdrawals, 2022: India holds 26.8% of the group total and ranks 1 of 15. Source: World Bank API ER.H2O.FWTL.K3 (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Withdrawals as Share of Internal Resources
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2022
indicators.details:
What it shows — Freshwater withdrawals as a percentage of internal renewable resources. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 44.78% in 2022. Above 40% signals high water stress.

Why it matters — Water stress affects farm output and city supply.

datasets.label: Withdrawals as Share of Internal Resources

series.note: Withdrawals as Share of Internal Resources: India's annual series, 1980 to 2022; the latest value is 44.78%. Source: World Bank API ER.H2O.FWTL.ZS (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.details:

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2022; India ranks 3 of 15 (1 = highest value). Above 40% signals high water stress.

Why it matters — Water stress affects farm output and city supply.

datasets.label: Withdrawals as Share of Internal Resources: Peer Ranking (2022)

series.note: Withdrawals as Share of Internal Resources, 2022: India ranks 3 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API ER.H2O.FWTL.ZS (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Renewable Water per Person: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:
What it shows — Internal renewable freshwater resources per person. This chart overlays India with 6 comparison countries.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. Below 1,700 m3 is water stress; below 1,000 is scarcity.

Why it matters — India is edging toward scarcity levels as population grows.

series.note: Renewable Water per Person: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API ER.H2O.INTR.PC (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Renewable Water per Person: Peer Ranking (2022)
indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2022
indicators.details:
What it shows — Internal renewable freshwater resources per person. Fifteen countries are ranked on the latest year with broad coverage.

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2022; India ranks 12 of 15 (1 = highest value). Below 1,700 m3 is water stress; below 1,000 is scarcity.

Why it matters — India is edging toward scarcity levels as population grows.

datasets.label: Renewable Water per Person: Peer Ranking (2022)

series.note: Renewable Water per Person, 2022: India ranks 12 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API ER.H2O.INTR.PC (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Water Productivity
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2022
indicators.details:
What it shows — Constant GDP produced per cubic metre of freshwater withdrawn. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 4.62 GDP $ per m3 in 2022. A rising line means more output per drop of water.

Why it matters — Water productivity measures efficiency gains in a water-scarce country.

series.note: Water Productivity: India's annual series, 1980 to 2022; the latest value is 4.62 GDP $ per m3. Source: World Bank API ER.GDP.FWTL.M3.KD (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:
What it shows — Constant GDP produced per cubic metre of freshwater withdrawn. This chart overlays India with 6 comparison countries.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. A rising line means more output per drop of water.

Why it matters — Water productivity measures efficiency gains in a water-scarce country.

series.note: Water Productivity: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API ER.GDP.FWTL.M3.KD (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: India: Freshwater Withdrawals by Sector (2022)
indicators.subtitle: India, shares of total, 2022
indicators.details:
What it shows — Shares of India's freshwater withdrawals that go to farms, factories and households.

How to read it — Agriculture dominates the slice, so irrigation efficiency matters most. In 2022, Agriculture is the largest slice at 90.4%.

Why it matters — Sector shares show where water-saving policy would have the biggest effect.

series.note: India: Freshwater Withdrawals by Sector, 2022: Agriculture is the largest slice at 90.4%. Source: World Bank API ER.H2O.FWAG.ZS, ER.H2O.FWIN.ZS, ER.H2O.FWDM.ZS (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Average Annual Precipitation
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2022
indicators.details:
What it shows — Long-term average rainfall depth across the country. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 1,083 mm in 2022. India's rainfall is mostly monsoon-borne.

Why it matters — Rainfall underpins water supply and agricultural output.

series.note: Average Annual Precipitation: India's annual series, 1980 to 2022; the latest value is 1,083 mm. Source: World Bank API AG.LND.PRCP.MM (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2022

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2022; India ranks 8 of 15 (1 = highest value). India's rainfall is mostly monsoon-borne.

Why it matters — Rainfall underpins water supply and agricultural output.

series.note: Average Annual Precipitation, 2022: India ranks 8 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API AG.LND.PRCP.MM (FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank); latest year with data: 2022.

indicators.title: Municipal Solid Waste Generated by State (2021-22)
indicators.subtitle: Tonnes per day (CPCB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much municipal solid waste (household and commercial garbage) each State's urban local bodies generate per day, as reported to the Central Pollution Control Board.

How to read it — Longer bars mean more waste each day. Populous, urbanised States such as Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Delhi generate the most.

Why it matters — Waste volumes set the scale of collection, processing and landfill capacity cities need under the Solid Waste Management Rules and Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban).

datasets.label: Municipal Solid Waste Generated by State (2021-22)

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 80 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2021-22. Ranked highest to lowest. Values are shown as published; Uttarakhand's reported figure is unusually high relative to its population.

indicators.title: Urban Waste: Generated, Collected, Treated, Landfilled (2021-22)
indicators.subtitle: All-India municipal solid waste, tonnes per day (CPCB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — All-India totals of municipal solid waste generated, collected, scientifically treated and sent to landfill each day.

How to read it — Read the bars left to right as a funnel: the gap between Generated and Collected is waste left on streets, and the gap between Collected and Treated is waste dumped without processing.

Why it matters — The treated share is the clearest measure of whether cities are actually managing waste rather than just moving it to dumpsites.

datasets.label: Urban Waste: Generated, Collected, Treated, Landfilled (2021-22)

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 80 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). Latest period reported: 2021-22. All-India figures are the sum of State/UT reports for the latest year.

indicators.title: Plastic Waste Generated
indicators.subtitle: Estimated plastic waste, tonnes per annum (CPCB)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Estimated plastic waste generated across India each year, summed from State Pollution Control Board reports to the CPCB.

How to read it — Bars show the national total. Jumps can reflect better reporting by States as well as real growth in plastic use.

Why it matters — Plastic waste clogs drains, pollutes rivers and seas and is the target of India's single-use plastic ban and Extended Producer Responsibility rules.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 132 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). National totals are the sum of State/UT estimates.

indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024

How to read it — The line ends at 3,153.8 Mt CO2e in 2024. Bigger bars or slices are bigger absolute emitters.

Why it matters — India's rank shows its weight in global climate outcomes.

series.note: CO2 Emissions: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 3,153.8 Mt CO2e. Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.CO2.MT.CE.AR5 (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

Why it matters — India's rank shows its weight in global climate outcomes.

How to read it — The line ends at 861.61 Mt CO2e in 2024. Rising lines show growth in livestock and rice farming.

Why it matters — Methane is a potent short-lived warming gas where quick cuts pay off.

series.note: Methane Emissions: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 861.61 Mt CO2e. Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.CH4.MT.CE.AR5 (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

series.note: Methane Emissions, 2024: India ranks 2 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API EN.GHG.CH4.MT.CE.AR5 (EDGAR / CAIT / World Bank climate data); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Fertiliser Use per Hectare
indicators.subtitle: Kg of N+P+K nutrients per hectare of arable land
indicators.details:
What it shows — How intensively Indian farmland is fertilised: kilograms of nitrogen, phosphate and potash applied per hectare.

How to read it — A rising line means more intensive farming. Compare it with cereal yields to see whether extra fertiliser still raises output.

Why it matters — Heavy, unbalanced fertiliser use raises the subsidy bill and degrades soil and groundwater, which is why soil-health cards and nano-urea are being promoted.

series.note: Kg of N+P+K nutrients per hectare of arable land. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator AG.CON.FERT.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Irrigated Agricultural Land
indicators.subtitle: Share of agricultural land that is irrigated, %
indicators.details:
What it shows — The share of India's agricultural land that receives irrigation rather than depending only on rain.

How to read it — Higher means farming is better protected from monsoon failures.

Why it matters — Irrigation is the biggest buffer against drought; PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana aims to extend it to every farm.

series.note: Share of agricultural land that is irrigated, %. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator AG.LND.IRIG.AG.ZS); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Arable Land per Person
indicators.subtitle: Hectares of arable land per person
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much cropland India has for each person.

How to read it — The line falls as population grows on a fixed land base; fragmentation means the average farm holding is now about one hectare.

Why it matters — Shrinking land per person makes productivity growth, not area expansion, the only route to feeding more people.

series.note: Hectares of arable land per person. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator AG.LND.ARBL.HA.PC); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Food Production Index
indicators.subtitle: Index of food output, 2014-2016 = 100
indicators.details:
What it shows — A volume index of all food crops and livestock produced in India, set to 100 for 2014-2016.

How to read it — A value of 120 means 20% more food than the 2014-16 average. Steady growth with few dips shows resilient farm output.

Why it matters — It summarises whether food supply is keeping pace with population and demand.

series.note: Index of food output, 2014-2016 = 100. Official national statistics compiled by the World Bank (indicator AG.PRD.FOOD.XD); gaps reflect years without a reported value.

indicators.title: Foodgrain Production
indicators.subtitle: Million tonnes (Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare)
indicators.details:
What it shows — India's production of rice, wheat, coarse cereals (millets, maize) and pulses, and their total, for each crop year (July-June).

How to read it — The top line is total foodgrains; the lines below show what it is made of. Dips usually follow drought years such as 2009-10 and 2014-15.

Why it matters — Foodgrain output underpins food security, the public distribution system (PDS) and food inflation. Pulses matter because India still imports to meet demand.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 51 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Oilseed Production
indicators.subtitle: Lakh tonnes (Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Production of India's nine major oilseeds and the three biggest of them: soybean, rapeseed-mustard and groundnut.

How to read it — Compare the total with the three crops below it to see which crop is driving growth or decline.

Why it matters — India imports more than half of its edible oil, so domestic oilseed output decides the import bill and is the target of the National Mission on Edible Oils.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 51 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). The API labels these rows 'Million tonnes', but the magnitudes match the Ministry's lakh-tonne series (for example 2023-24 nine oilseeds = 416.7 lakh tonnes).

indicators.title: Sugarcane Production
indicators.subtitle: Lakh tonnes (Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total sugarcane harvested in India in each crop year.

How to read it — Higher values mean a bigger cane crop; the swings follow monsoon rainfall and irrigation in Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka.

Why it matters — Sugarcane feeds the sugar industry and the ethanol-blending programme, but it is very water-intensive, which ties it to groundwater depletion debates.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 51 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/). The API labels these rows 'Million tonnes', but the magnitudes match the Ministry's lakh-tonne series (2023-24 = 4,351 lakh tonnes, about 435 million tonnes).

indicators.title: Fertiliser Consumption by Nutrient
indicators.subtitle: Lakh tonnes of N, P and K (Department of Fertilizers)
indicators.details:
What it shows — How much nitrogen, phosphate and potash fertiliser Indian farmers used each year since 1981-82, in nutrient terms.

How to read it — Nitrogen (mostly urea) towers over the others. The agronomic ideal is roughly 4:2:1 for N:P:K, so a widening gap signals unbalanced use.

Why it matters — Fertiliser subsidies are one of the largest items in the Union Budget, and overuse of urea degrades soil and water; this chart shows the scale of both.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 54 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Fertiliser: Consumption vs Production vs Imports
indicators.subtitle: Total N+P+K, lakh tonnes (Department of Fertilizers)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total fertiliser nutrients consumed in India against what was produced domestically and what was imported.

How to read it — When the consumption line sits above production, the gap is filled by imports. Watch whether new urea plants narrow that gap.

Why it matters — Import dependence exposes farmers and the subsidy bill to global gas and fertiliser prices, as in 2022.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 54 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Livestock Population by Species
indicators.subtitle: Million animals, Livestock Census (DAHD)
indicators.details:
What it shows — The number of cattle, buffaloes, goats, sheep and pigs counted in each Livestock Census since 1951.

How to read it — Each point is a census year. Cattle numbers have plateaued while buffaloes and goats have grown, reflecting the shift to dairy and meat.

Why it matters — Livestock supports about a fifth of rural households and makes India the world's largest milk producer.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 61 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Fish Production: Inland vs Marine
indicators.subtitle: Lakh tonnes (Department of Fisheries)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Fish produced in India each year from inland waters (rivers, reservoirs and fish farms) and from the sea.

How to read it — Inland production overtook marine catch in the 1990s and now dominates; that is the aquaculture boom.

Why it matters — India is the world's second-largest fish producer, and fisheries support millions of coastal and rural livelihoods and a major seafood-export trade.

series.note: Source: MoSPI EnviStats India, indicator 64 on the MoSPI API platform (https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/).

indicators.title: Cereal Production
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total harvested production of wheat, rice, maize and other cereals. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 391.12 million tonnes in 2024. Bigger bars or slices are larger producers.

Why it matters — Cereals are the backbone of India's food supply.

series.note: Cereal Production: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 391.12 million tonnes. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Cereal Production: Peer Ranking (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total harvested production of wheat, rice, maize and other cereals. Fifteen countries are ranked on the latest year with broad coverage.

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2024; India ranks 3 of 15 (1 = highest value). Bigger bars or slices are larger producers.

Why it matters — Cereals are the backbone of India's food supply.

series.note: Cereal Production, 2024: India ranks 3 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Cereal Production: Share Among Peers (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Each country's share of the 15-country total
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total harvested production of wheat, rice, maize and other cereals. Slices show each country's share of the sampled countries' total.

How to read it — Slices are shares of the group total in 2024; India holds 18.6% and ranks 3 of 15. A bigger slice means a larger absolute amount, not a better outcome.

Why it matters — Cereals are the backbone of India's food supply.

series.note: Cereal Production, 2024: India holds 18.6% of the group total and ranks 3 of 15. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Crop Production Index (2014-16 = 100)
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Index of crop output relative to a 2014-2016 base. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 129.64 index in 2024. A rising line means crop output is growing faster.

Why it matters — The index tracks output growth beyond land expansion.

series.note: Crop Production Index (2014-16 = 100): India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 129.64 index. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CROP.XD (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Crop Production Index (2014-16 = 100): India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:
What it shows — Index of crop output relative to a 2014-2016 base. This chart overlays India with 6 comparison countries.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. A rising line means crop output is growing faster.

Why it matters — The index tracks output growth beyond land expansion.

series.note: Crop Production Index (2014-16 = 100): India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CROP.XD (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Cereal Yield: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:
What it shows — Cereal output per hectare of harvested land. This chart overlays India with 6 comparison countries.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. Higher bars show more intensive farming.

Why it matters — Yield gaps between India and the leaders show scope for productivity growth.

series.note: Cereal Yield: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API AG.YLD.CREL.KG (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Cereal Yield: Peer Ranking (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2024

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2024; India ranks 12 of 15 (1 = highest value). Higher bars show more intensive farming.

Why it matters — Yield gaps between India and the leaders show scope for productivity growth.

series.note: Cereal Yield, 2024: India ranks 12 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API AG.YLD.CREL.KG (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Cereal Production per Person
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Cereal production divided by population, derived from two official series. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 269.57 kg per person in 2024. A rising line means harvests are outpacing population.

Why it matters — Per-person output shows food self-reliance.

series.note: Cereal Production per Person: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 269.57 kg per person. Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT, SP.POP.TOTL (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

How to read it — Bars run from highest to lowest in 2024; India ranks 10 of 15 (1 = highest value). A rising line means harvests are outpacing population.

datasets.label: Cereal Production per Person: Peer Ranking (2024)

series.note: Cereal Production per Person, 2024: India ranks 10 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API AG.PRD.CREL.MT, SP.POP.TOTL (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2025

Why it matters — It shows how much farm output is expanding in real terms.

series.note: Agriculture Value Added: India's annual series, 1980 to 2025; the latest value is 531.67 USD bn (2015 prices). Source: World Bank API NV.AGR.TOTL.KD (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

Why it matters — It shows how much farm output is expanding in real terms.

series.note: Agriculture Value Added, 2025: India ranks 2 of 13 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API NV.AGR.TOTL.KD (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Land Under Cereal Production
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Area harvested for cereals. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 107.67 million hectares in 2024. A flat line while production rises means yield gains.

Why it matters — Cereal area shows land constraints on food growth.

series.note: Land Under Cereal Production: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 107.67 million hectares. Source: World Bank API AG.LND.CREL.HA (FAO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Food Exports: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. Higher bars show food-export dependence.

Why it matters — India's food export share indicates its role in feeding the world.

series.note: Food Exports: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API TX.VAL.FOOD.ZS.UN (FAO / WTO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Food Exports: Peer Ranking (2025)
indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2025

Why it matters — India's food export share indicates its role in feeding the world.

series.note: Food Exports, 2025: India ranks 7 of 12 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API TX.VAL.FOOD.ZS.UN (FAO / WTO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Food Imports: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. Higher bars show food-import dependence.

Why it matters — Low food-import share signals self-sufficiency.

series.note: Food Imports: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API TM.VAL.FOOD.ZS.UN (FAO / WTO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Food Imports: Peer Ranking (2025)
indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2025

series.note: Food Imports, 2025: India ranks 12 of 12 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API TM.VAL.FOOD.ZS.UN (FAO / WTO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2025.

indicators.title: Agricultural Land: India vs Peers
indicators.subtitle: India against major economies and neighbours
indicators.details:
What it shows — Agricultural land as a share of total land area. This chart overlays India with 6 comparison countries.

How to read it — India is the orange line; the others are China, United States, Japan, Germany, Brazil, Bangladesh. India has one of the highest shares globally.

Why it matters — High land use leaves little room for further farm expansion.

series.note: Agricultural Land: India against 6 comparison countries; gaps are years without a reported value. Source: World Bank API AG.LND.AGRI.ZS (FAO / WTO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Agricultural Land: Peer Ranking (2024)
indicators.subtitle: Countries ranked highest to lowest, 2024

series.note: Agricultural Land, 2024: India ranks 4 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API AG.LND.AGRI.ZS (FAO / WTO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Arable Land
indicators.subtitle: India, 1980-2024

How to read it — The line ends at 51.73% of land area in 2024. A flat line means no new land is being ploughed.

Why it matters — Arable land is the natural ceiling on production.

series.note: Arable Land: India's annual series, 1980 to 2024; the latest value is 51.73% of land area. Source: World Bank API AG.LND.ARBL.ZS (FAO / WTO / World Bank); latest year with data: 2024.

indicators.title: Defence expenditure
indicators.subtitle: Military expenditure as share of GDP
indicators.details:
Military expenditure tracks defence spending relative to the size of the national economy. It measures military resource allocation across peacetime and security challenges.

Data comes through the World Bank open API and SIPRI military expenditure database.

indicators.title: India defence exports
indicators.subtitle: Annual defence exports from India
indicators.details:
India's defence exports have expanded significantly as part of indigenous manufacturing and Make in India defence initiatives.

Data is collated from official Ministry of Defence Department of Defence Production (DDP) statistics.

series.source: Ministry of Defence, Department of Defence Production (DDP); India Defence Exports in INR Crores

indicators.title: Value of defence production
indicators.subtitle: Total value of indigenous defence production
indicators.details:
Total value of defence production captures manufacturing output across Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs), ordnance factories, and private sector defence enterprises.

Official data is published by the Department of Defence Production, Ministry of Defence.

series.source: Ministry of Defence (DDP) annual report statistics; Value of Indigenous Defence Production in INR Crores

indicators.title: Defence stockpile index
indicators.subtitle: SIPRI arms inventory & capability index
indicators.details:
SIPRI Trend Indicator Value (TIV) measures the volume of conventional military capability and major weapons stockpiles transferred and maintained.

It provides a long-run comparative measure of military equipment inventory.

series.source: Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) Arms Transfers Database & Stockpile TIV Index

indicators.title: Defence production & exports engine
indicators.subtitle: Defence production vs exports trajectory
indicators.details:
This combined graph compares total indigenous defence production alongside defence export growth in INR Crores.

It illustrates the structural transition of India's defence industrial base toward export competitiveness.

series.source: Ministry of Defence (DDP) open statistics; Total Defence Production vs Defence Exports in INR Crores

indicators.title: Defence allocation
indicators.subtitle: Share of total Union budget expenditure
indicators.details:
Defence allocation tracks military budget spending as a percentage of overall Central Government Expenditure.

Data is collated from official Ministry of Finance Union Budget allocation documents.

series.source: Union Budget of India Documents & Ministry of Finance Budget Allocation Data (% of Total Central Expenditure)

indicators.title: Defence R&D expenditure
indicators.subtitle: DRDO & defense research spending
indicators.details:
Defence R&D expenditure measures capital and revenue allocation for indigenous weapons development, missile technology, and military research.

Data is sourced from DRDO and Ministry of Defence annual standing committee reports.

series.source: DRDO Annual Reports & Ministry of Defence R&D Expenditure (INR Crores)

indicators.title: Defence modernization capital outlay
indicators.subtitle: Capital acquisition spending for armed forces
indicators.details:
Capital acquisition outlay reflects funds allocated for procuring weapons, aircraft, naval frigates, artillery, and modern military hardware.

Official statistics are published by the Ministry of Defence.

series.source: Ministry of Defence Capital Outlay Statements & Parliamentary Standing Committee Reports (INR Crores)

indicators.title: India arms imports trend
indicators.subtitle: SIPRI arms import Trend Indicator Value (TIV)
indicators.details: SIPRI arms imports index tracks conventional weapon import volumes. The declining trend highlights India's structural shift from foreign import dependency toward indigenous manufacturing.

series.source: SIPRI Arms Transfers Database (Trend Indicator Value - TIV)

indicators.title: LWE civilian casualties
indicators.subtitle: Civilians killed in Maoist insurgency violence
indicators.details:
MHA describes civilian and security-force casualties in LWE violence, but the current public page does not expose a stable annual category table.

This series is sourced from the South Asia Terrorism Portal (SATP), a secondary, non-official source that compiles a year-wise civilian/security-force/perpetrator breakdown from news reports for its Maoist Insurgency tracker. It uses a different classification and count than MHA's own 2004-2025 aggregate of 8,956 deaths, so the two figures should not be summed or treated as the same series.

series.note: South Asia Terrorism Portal (secondary, non-official source) 'Maoist Insurgency' fatality breakdown, not MHA's own category data. MHA's public page only publishes the 2004-2025 aggregate (8,956 deaths) without this breakdown.

indicators.title: Districts affected by Left-Wing Extremism
indicators.subtitle: Approximate number of LWE-affected districts, peak to 2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — How many districts the Ministry of Home Affairs treated as affected by Maoist violence at successive reviews, from the 2011-12 peak.

How to read it — The count fell from 223 to 126 by 2014 and to 38 by April 2024; the 2018 and 2021 points are approximate.

Why it matters — The district count is the official yardstick for how far the Red Corridor has shrunk.

series.note: ICFS "Closing the Red Corridor" (Shruti Kapil, 2026), Figure 5 and text (223 districts at peak, 126 in 2014, 38 in April 2024); ORF "Reclaiming the Heartland" gives the same 223 districts for 2011-12. The 2018 (about 90) and 2021 (about 70) values are read from an unlabelled chart and are approximate. The sources disagree on the 2026 count (PIB reports none, ORF and ICFS report two), so 2026 is not plotted.
series.source: International Centre for Sustainability and Futures (https://icfs.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Closing-The-Red-Corridor_Oct-26.pdf)

indicators.title: Most-affected LWE districts
indicators.subtitle: Districts classed as most affected by Left-Wing Extremism
indicators.details:
What it shows — Districts in the most severely affected category.

How to read it — The count went from 35 in 2014 to zero in 2026.

Why it matters — These districts drove most of the violence and received the heaviest security deployment.

series.note: PIB backgrounder "Naxal-Free India: Integrated Strategies Defeated Left-Wing Extremism" (Ministry of Home Affairs, 1 August 2026): 35 most-affected districts in 2014 and none by 2026.

indicators.title: Naxal-related violent incidents
indicators.subtitle: Incidents in 2010, 2014 and 2026 (to 29 July)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Violent incidents attributed to Left-Wing Extremism in three reference years.

How to read it — 2010 was the deadliest year; 2026 shows 33 incidents so far.

Why it matters — The headline measure of how violent the insurgency has been.

series.note: PIB backgrounder "Naxal-Free India: Integrated Strategies Defeated Left-Wing Extremism" (Ministry of Home Affairs, 1 August 2026). 2026 is a part-year figure as on 29 July 2026. The decade 2004-14 recorded 17,542 violent incidents in total.

indicators.title: Naxal-related fatalities
indicators.subtitle: Total fatalities in 2010, 2014 and 2026 (to 29 July)
indicators.details:
What it shows — Deaths of civilians, security forces and cadres in LWE-related violence.

How to read it — Fatalities fell from 1,005 in 2010 to 310 in 2014 and 11 in 2026 so far.

Why it matters — Fatalities show the human cost behind the incident counts.

series.note: PIB backgrounder "Naxal-Free India: Integrated Strategies Defeated Left-Wing Extremism" (Ministry of Home Affairs, 1 August 2026). 2026 is a part-year figure as on 29 July 2026. Over 2004-14 the report counts 1,913 security-force deaths and 5,019 civilian deaths.

indicators.title: Civilians killed by Maoists
indicators.subtitle: Civilian deaths in 2010, 2014 and 2024
indicators.details:
What it shows — Civilians killed in Maoist violence in three reference years.

How to read it — Civilian deaths fell by more than 80 percent between 2010 and 2024.

Why it matters — Civilian safety is the clearest sign of state control in the affected districts.

series.note: ICFS "Closing the Red Corridor" (Shruti Kapil, 2026), Figure 8 (Ministry of Home Affairs data). PIB confirms 720 civilian deaths in 2010.
series.source: International Centre for Sustainability and Futures (https://icfs.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Closing-The-Red-Corridor_Oct-26.pdf)

indicators.title: Maoist attacks on economic infrastructure
indicators.subtitle: Attacks on roads, rail, telecom and other infrastructure
indicators.details:
What it shows — Incidents of Maoist damage to economic infrastructure.

How to read it — Attacks fell from 365 in 2010 to 25 in 2024.

Why it matters — Roads, towers and rail lines are what opened the interior to development.

series.note: ICFS "Closing the Red Corridor" (Shruti Kapil, 2026), Figure 8 (Ministry of Home Affairs data).
series.source: International Centre for Sustainability and Futures (https://icfs.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Closing-The-Red-Corridor_Oct-26.pdf)

indicators.title: Maoists surrendering each year
indicators.subtitle: Cadres who surrendered, 2004 to March 2026
indicators.details:
What it shows — Maoist cadres who laid down arms in each year.

How to read it — Surrenders spiked in 2005-06 and 2016 and reached 2,337 in 2025.

Why it matters — Surrender trends show whether rehabilitation policy is eroding the insurgency from within.

series.note: ICFS "Closing the Red Corridor" (Shruti Kapil, 2026), Figure 9 (labelled annual data). 2026 covers 1 January to 30 March only. The PIB backgrounder reports 3,927 surrenders between 2024 and March 2026.
series.source: International Centre for Sustainability and Futures (https://icfs.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Closing-The-Red-Corridor_Oct-26.pdf)

indicators.title: Security build-up in LWE areas
indicators.subtitle: Fortified police stations, new CAPF camps and night-landing helipads
indicators.details:

indicators.title: Terrorist attacks

indicators.title: Intentional homicide rate
indicators.subtitle: Intentional homicides per 100,000 people
indicators.details:
The intentional homicide rate is a broad violence indicator measuring deaths caused by another person per 100,000 population. It is useful as a long-run public-safety context signal, but it does not cover every violent incident.

The World Bank series provides modern historical coverage and should be interpreted alongside NCRB crime data, whose definitions and reporting systems vary by year.

indicators.title: NCRB crime indicators
indicators.subtitle: Crime in India 2023 rates by category
indicators.details:
The National Crime Records Bureau publishes Crime in India tables covering reported offences, crime rates, and related public-safety measures. Editions are not consistently comparable across years, so this card shows a single-year (2023) snapshot across crime categories rather than a fabricated multi-year trend.

Values are official Crime in India 2023 rates per 100,000 population (per 100,000 children for crimes against children), compiled and cited on Wikipedia from NCRB Crime in India 2023 Volumes I-III.

series.note: NCRB Crime in India 2023 rates per 100,000 population by category (per 100,000 children for crimes against children), compiled from official Crime in India 2023 Volumes I-III. A single-year snapshot, not a multi-year trend, because NCRB editions are not consistently comparable across years.

indicators.title: Overall violent incidents
indicators.subtitle: Comparable all-India incident series
indicators.details:
No single official open series currently combines violent crime, Maoist violence, and terrorism consistently across India.

This card stays visible as a research target so the dashboard does not add incompatible NCRB, MHA, and GTD definitions into a misleading total.

series.note: Total reported IPC cognizable violent crime cases across India (murder, attempt to murder, rape, kidnapping, dacoity, robbery, rioting).

series.note: Total reported cognizable IPC crime rate per 100,000 population across official Crime in India annual reports.

indicators.title: 2022 State Assembly: Effective Candidates per Seat by State
indicators.subtitle: Mean constituency effective number of candidates
indicators.details:
What it shows — Mean constituency-level effective number of candidates for each state/UT.

How to read it — A seat's value is 1 divided by the sum of squared candidate vote shares; larger values indicate votes are spread across more candidates.

Why it matters — Complements raw candidate-count charts with a vote-weighted measure of electoral competition.

datasets.label: 2022 State Assembly: Effective Candidates per Seat by State

series.note: For each state/UT in the 2022 State Assembly results, calculates the effective number of candidates in each seat as 1 / sum(candidate vote-share squared), then averages those seat values. NOTA and seats without at least two candidates with reported votes are excluded. This competition measure is distinct from raw candidate counts in the existing election indices.
series.source: Election Commission of India candidate results (data/recent-indian-elections.json)

indicators.title: Assam 2021: Victory Margin Distribution
indicators.subtitle: Contested seats grouped by winner's share lead
indicators.details:
What it shows — Distribution of winning candidates' vote leads over the runner-up by constituency.

How to read it — The denominator is the sum of listed non-NOTA candidate votes; values are grouped in percentage-point bands.

Why it matters — Shows how often archived contests were close or decisive without reusing the 2024/2022–2026 index charts.

series.note: Uses candidate-level rows in the partial ECI historical archive for Assam (2021). Available reports are selected downloads, not a complete national or state-time series. Margin is (winner votes minus runner-up votes) divided by listed non-NOTA candidate votes; seats without two reported candidate vote totals are excluded.
series.source: Election Commission of India statistical reports and detailed-result XLSX downloads (data/historical-elections.json)

indicators.title: 2018 Presidential Candidate Total Receipts
indicators.subtitle: President candidate campaign-finance totals by party
indicators.details:
Federal Election Commission candidate-summary totals for the 2018 filing cycle. Total Receipts are aggregated by candidate party. Presidential candidate totals use party as the grouping because the FEC summary file does not report state presidential vote totals. The 2018, 2022 and 2026 filing cycles are midterm years, not Presidential election years.

These are campaign-finance amounts, not votes, turnout, or public contributions alone. Candidate summaries include authorized committees and may be revised when amended reports are processed.

indicators.title: Presidential Campaign Receipts by FEC Cycle
indicators.subtitle: Sum of listed candidate/state aggregates for presidential office
indicators.details:
What it shows — Total listed receipts for Presidential candidate summaries in each FEC cycle.

How to read it — Compare displayed nominal totals only; candidate/state coverage and election type differ between cycles.

Why it matters — Shows the scale and direction of campaign-finance aggregates across the available FEC cycles.

datasets.label: Presidential Campaign Receipts by FEC Cycle

series.note: For each cycle, sums the values in the committed FEC presidential receipts series. Nominal amounts are not inflation-adjusted; cycle length and candidate coverage differ. The 2026 election cycle is ongoing and reporting is incomplete.
series.source: Federal Election Commission candidate summary bulk files (data/us-campaign-finance.json)

indicators.title: Presidential Campaign Receipts Cycle Growth
indicators.subtitle: Nominal percentage change between adjacent available FEC cycles
indicators.details:
What it shows — Percentage change in the listed nominal aggregate between adjacent FEC cycles.

How to read it — Positive values indicate a higher later-cycle total; negative values indicate a lower total.

Why it matters — Provides a relative comparison alongside nominal dollar totals.

series.note: Calculated as (later cycle total / prior available cycle total − 1) × 100. No inflation adjustment is applied; cycles differ in coverage and duration, and a zero or missing baseline is omitted.
series.source: Federal Election Commission candidate summary bulk files (data/us-campaign-finance.json)

indicators.title: Travel Expenditures Abroad
indicators.subtitle: India, 1995-2020
indicators.details:
What it shows — Spending by residents on travel abroad, balance-of-payments basis. This chart follows India's annual series.

How to read it — The line ends at 12.57 USD bn in 2020. Rising lines show growing outbound tourism.

Why it matters — Outbound travel spending is a leakage of foreign exchange.

series.note: Travel Expenditures Abroad: India's annual series, 1995 to 2020; the latest value is 12.57 USD bn. Source: World Bank API ST.INT.TVLX.CD (IMF Balance of Payments / UN Tourism via World Bank); latest year with data: 2020.

Why it matters — Outbound travel spending is a leakage of foreign exchange.

series.note: Travel Expenditures Abroad, 2020: India ranks 6 of 15 (1 = highest value). Source: World Bank API ST.INT.TVLX.CD (IMF Balance of Payments / UN Tourism via World Bank); latest year with data: 2020.

indicators.title: All-Time Medals by Multi-Sport Event
indicators.subtitle: India's gold, silver and bronze across the four major multi-sport Games
indicators.details:
What it shows — India's all-time medal haul at each of the four major multi-sport events, split by medal colour.

How to read it — Each group of bars is one event; compare heights to see where India wins most and how golds compare with silvers and bronzes.

Why it matters — Regional Games are far less competitive than the Olympics, so medal counts are only comparable within an event, not across them.

series.note: Summer Olympics, Summer Paralympics, Asian Games (to Aichi–Nagoya 2026) and Commonwealth Games (to Glasgow 2026), from the IOC, IPC, OCA and CGF records. Recent editions were checked against IPC result pages and PIB (Government of India) releases.

indicators.title: Medals by Sport Across All Major Games
indicators.subtitle: Total medals in each of the 38 sports India has medalled in, by event
indicators.details:
What it shows — Every sport in which India has won a medal at the Olympics, Paralympics, Asian Games or Commonwealth Games.

How to read it — Bars are split by event; hover a bar to see how many medals each Games contributed.

Why it matters — Shooting, wrestling, athletics, weightlifting and boxing carry India's medal tally across every level of competition.

series.note: Sum of gold, silver and bronze from the IOC, IPC, OCA and CGF medals-by-sport tables. Sports beyond the top 24 are combined. The OCA and CGF per-sport splits are one medal short of the official 2022 edition tallies (one Hangzhou bronze, one Birmingham gold).

How to read it — Each year is one Games. Every gold before 2008 came in men's field hockey; individual medals arrive at every Games from 1996.

Why it matters — Shows the shift from a single-sport hockey dynasty to a broader base in shooting, wrestling, badminton, boxing and athletics.

series.note: IOC official results database; Paris 2024 (0/1/5) and Tokyo 2020 (1/2/4) are confirmed by olympics.com and PIB (PRID 2045963). Summer Games only; India has not won a Winter Olympic medal. 1904, 1908 and 1912 had no Indian team; 1940 and 1944 were cancelled.

indicators.title: Olympic Medals by Sport
indicators.subtitle: India's 41 Summer Olympic medals by sport and colour
indicators.details:
What it shows — All 41 of India's Olympic medals grouped by sport.

How to read it — Field hockey holds 8 of India's 10 golds; the other two came in shooting (2008) and athletics (2020).

Why it matters — Highlights where Olympic success has been concentrated and where it is spreading.

series.note: IOC official results database; Paris 2024 (0/1/5) and Tokyo 2020 (1/2/4) are confirmed by olympics.com and PIB (PRID 2045963). Summer Games only; India has not won a Winter Olympic medal. 1904, 1908 and 1912 had no Indian team; 1940 and 1944 were cancelled.

indicators.title: Olympic Medal Colour Split

What it shows — How India's Olympic medals divide between gold, silver and bronze.

How to read it — Slices show each colour's share; hover for counts.

Why it matters — Half of India's medals are bronze, a sign of podium depth rather than event dominance.

series.note: IOC official results database; Paris 2024 (0/1/5) and Tokyo 2020 (1/2/4) are confirmed by olympics.com and PIB (PRID 2045963). Summer Games only; India has not won a Winter Olympic medal. 1904, 1908 and 1912 had no Indian team; 1940 and 1944 were cancelled.

indicators.details:

How to read it — Contingents passed 100 for the first time in Rio 2016.

Why it matters — Qualification breadth is a leading indicator for medal counts.

indicators.details:
What it shows — India's medals at every Summer Paralympics it has entered, from Tel Aviv 1968 to Paris 2024.

How to read it — Murlikant Petkar's 1972 swimming gold was the first; the surge comes after 2016.

Why it matters — India's Paralympic programme now wins more medals per Games than its Olympic one.

series.note: IPC historical results database. 1972, 1984, 2004, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024 were checked against the IPC medal standings pages. India did not compete in 1976 or 1980. Tokyo 2020 (19 medals) and Paris 2024 (29) account for most of the 60-medal total.

indicators.title: Paralympic Medals by Sport
indicators.subtitle: India's 60 Summer Paralympic medals by sport and colour
indicators.details:
What it shows — All 60 of India's Paralympic medals grouped by sport.

How to read it — Athletics (javelin, high jump, club and discus throws) supplies well over half of all medals.

Why it matters — Shows the sports where India's para-athletes have become world-class.

series.note: IPC historical results by sport. IPC confirms 8 athletics golds; the athletics split 8/15/12 is the one that reconciles with India's 60-medal IPC total.

indicators.details:
What it shows — India's medals at each Asian Games, from the inaugural 1951 New Delhi Games to 2026.

How to read it — Group heights track the size of India's haul; bronzes have grown fastest as the programme has expanded.

Why it matters — The Asian Games are India's main benchmark against China, Japan and Korea.

series.note: Olympic Council of Asia records. 2014, Hangzhou 2022 (28/38/41 — 107 medals, India's best) and Aichi–Nagoya 2026 are confirmed by PIB releases; for Jakarta 2018 the OCA table (16/23/31) is used, while a 2026 PIB summary lists 15/24/30 from before a medal reallocation.

Why it matters — Shows both the depth sports (athletics, shooting, wrestling, boxing) and the dominant niches (kabaddi, cricket).

series.note: Sorted by total medals.

Why it matters — Programme changes (for example, shooting's absence in 2022) move India's tally as much as performance does.
